Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 21, verse 5:

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿So let him bring us a sign, as the earlier ones were sent [with signs]﴾, their intent is the kind of sign, not its equivalent.

(Benefit)

If you say: "Zayd came to me, but (bal) 'Amr," then it has two meanings:

The first: you negated coming from Zayd and affirmed it for 'Amr. On this view, it is an idrab of negation (a turning away from the first statement to the second, negating the first).

The second: you affirmed coming for 'Amr just as you affirmed it for Zayd, and you used bal to negate restricting the statement to the first, not to negate the attribution to him, but to negate restricting the attribution to him alone. This is called idrab iqtisar (a turning that restricts), and it is more common in the Qur'an and elsewhere, such as His, the Exalted saying: ﴿Nay, they say: "Confused dreams! Nay, he has invented it! Nay, he is a poet!"﴾

And His saying: ﴿Nay, their knowledge of the Hereafter has failed. Nay, they are in doubt concerning it. Nay, they are blind to it﴾, and its like. This is called idrab, and a departure from one story to another.

If you say: "Zayd did not come to me, but (bal) 'Amr," then it has two meanings:

The first: you negated coming from Zayd and affirmed it for 'Amr. This is the view of the majority.

The second: you negated coming from both of them together, so you attributed to the second the ruling of the first. You ruled the first as negated, then you attributed this ruling to the second.

The verified position regarding this particle is that it is mentioned to establish what follows it, whether negation or affirmation. Its consideration concerns two matters: what precedes it and what follows it. Since many grammarians did not distinguish between these two considerations, much confusion arose in their discussions about its meaning. So we say: as for the ruling of what follows it, it is establishment and confirmation. It resembles the particle qad with a verb, and the bare focus of speech on what follows it is more important to them than concern with what precedes it. So His, the Exalted saying: ﴿Nay, you prefer the present life﴾

The intent is to establish this sentence, not to turn away from His saying: ﴿He has indeed succeeded who purifies himself, remembers the name of his Lord, and prays﴾

Likewise His saying: ﴿No! Nay, you do not honour the orphan﴾

The intent is to establish and confirm this negation, not to turn away from His saying: ﴿And you devour the inheritance greedily, and you love wealth with an immense love﴾

Likewise, when it occurs between two opposing sentences, it conveys the establishment of each of them, as in His saying: ﴿And do not think of those who were killed in the way of Allah as dead; nay, they are alive with their Lord﴾. So the intent is the establishment of both the command and the statement. Likewise your saying: "Do not strike Zayd, but strike 'Amr," and likewise: "Zayd did not stand, but 'Amr stood." In all of this it serves to establish two sentences. Likewise His, the Exalted saying: ﴿Is it other than Allah you call upon, if you are truthful? Nay, it is Him alone you call upon﴾

The meaning is that when this great matter befalls you, you do not call upon other than Allah, but upon Him alone. This is an establishment of the abandonment of their calling upon their idols and of their calling upon the true God alone. Thus it enters upon one established statement after another. The first sometimes has its establishment as a preparation for the second, as in His, the Exalted saying: ﴿Those are like cattle; nay, they are more astray﴾. And sometimes it is not a preparation, as in His, the Exalted saying: ﴿And if a Qur'an by which mountains were moved, or the earth were cleft, or the dead were addressed... nay, to Allah belongs the affair entirely﴾. And sometimes it enters upon an established statement after a rejected statement, as in His, the Exalted saying: ﴿And they say: "The Most Merciful has taken a son." Glory be to Him! Nay, they are honoured servants﴾

In such a case the meaning of idrab appears, and it is not intended as a turning away from the mention, but a turning away from what was mentioned, its negation, and its nullification. Sometimes it comes to establish a statement after a statement from which the speaker has retracted, either through error, or because an opinion has become evident, or because forgetfulness has occurred. All of this is either in the report or in the thing reported. An example of the first is your saying: "You are my slave; nay, my master." An example of the second: "A lightning flashed; nay, the light of a fire." An example of the third: "Take this; nay, that." An example of the fourth: "I drank honey; nay, milk." It also comes with repetition, intending by its subsequent element priority in attention and mention, without negating what preceded it, as in His, the Exalted saying: ﴿Nay, they said: "Confused dreams! Nay, he has invented it! Nay, he is a poet!"﴾

They did not intend to nullify what preceded each one, but intended the priority of the later one by attention and reliance upon it, while what preceded it remains established. Likewise His, the Exalted saying: ﴿And they do not perceive when they will be raised. Nay, their knowledge of the Hereafter has failed. Nay, they are in doubt concerning it. Nay, they are blind to it﴾

So the intent is not the negation of the failure of their knowledge of the Hereafter, nor the negation of their doubt concerning it. So reflect upon it.

Among its occurrences is its coming after an oath whose answer is not mentioned, so it includes the establishment and confirmation of what follows it; and this, together with the oath, includes the establishment and confirmation of what the oath was meant to affirm.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 21, verses 21–23:

Just as the heavens and the earth would be ruined if there were in them gods other than Him, glory be to Him, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿If there were in them gods other than Allah, they would both be ruined.﴾

Likewise, when the heart contains an object of worship other than Allah, exalted is He, it becomes corrupt with a corruption whose rectification is not hoped for, unless that object of worship is removed from the heart, and Allah alone becomes its god and its object of worship, the one it loves, hopes in, fears, relies upon, and turns to in repentance.

(Benefit)

Know that the subsistence of the heavens, the earth, and creation lies in their worship of the true God. If there were in them another god besides Allah, he would not be a true god, for the true God has no partner, no equal, and no like. If they were to worship other than Him, they would be utterly corrupted, since the cause of their rectification would be absent. Their rectification lies in the worship of the true God, just as they could not exist except by depending upon the one Lord, the Subduer. It is impossible for them to depend for their existence on two equal lords, and likewise it is impossible for them to depend for their continuance and rectification on two equal gods.

Having understood this, know that the servant's need to worship Allah alone, associating nothing with Him in love, fear, hope, reliance, action performed for Him, swearing by Him, vowing to Him, submission to Him, humbling oneself before Him, glorifying Him, prostrating to Him, and drawing near to Him, is greater than the body's need for its spirit and the eye's need for its light. Indeed, this need has no parallel by which it can be measured. The true reality of the servant is his spirit and his heart, and they have no rectification except through their God, besides whom there is no god. They find rest in this world only through His remembrance, and they are toiling toward Him with toil, so they will meet Him, and they must meet Him. They have no rectification except through loving Him, worshipping Him, His pleasure in them, and His honoring them. Even if the servant were to obtain from other than Allah all the pleasures and joys he could obtain, they would not last for him.

Rather, he moves from one kind to another and from one person to another. He enjoys something at one time and then is tormented by it at another time, without fail. Very often the thing he enjoys and takes pleasure in is not one that benefits him or gives him pleasure. It may even harm him to be connected to it and to have it near him, and it damages him. What he obtains through contact with it is of the same kind as what the mangy camel obtains from the pleasure of the nails that scratch it: they draw blood, tear the skin, and increase its harm, yet it prefers that because of the pleasure it finds in scratching. Likewise, what the heart suffers from the love of other than Allah is a torment upon it, a harm, and in reality a pain, whose pleasure does not exceed the pleasure of scratching the mange. The intelligent person weighs the two matters and prefers the weightier and more beneficial of them. Allah is the Granter of success and the Helper, and His is the conclusive proof, as He has the abundant blessing.

The point is that the god of the servant, whom he cannot do without at every state, every moment, and every blink of an eye, is the true God, and everything other than Him is false. He is wherever the servant is, and the servant's dependence on Him and need for Him cannot be compared to any dependence or need. Rather, it is above every dependence and greater than every need. For this reason the leader of the ḥanīfs (the monotheists who turned away from false worship) said: ﴿I do not love those that set.﴾ [al-An'am: 76]. And Allah knows best.

(Benefit)

Consider how the verse was brought in denouncing those who take, besides Him, gods that do not equal Him, and yet they equate them with Him despite the greatest difference.

His saying ﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾ establishes the reality of divinity and singles Him out for lordship and divinity.

His saying ﴿but they are questioned﴾ refers to the state of those gods taken as deities: they are questioned, they are lorded over, and they are managed.

How, then, can they be equated with Him despite the greatest distinction?

This is the matter the speech was brought to address. The Jabriyyah (a determinist sect that denies human agency) took them as a refuge and a stronghold in denying His wisdom and in explaining His acts by their praiseworthy purposes and their sound outcomes.

And Allah is the Granter of success in what is right.

[Section: Love Is the Origin of Motion]

Every motion in the upper and lower worlds has love as its origin, and it is by love that they have their agency and their final purpose. This is because motions are of three kinds: voluntary motion that proceeds from will and choice, natural motion, and forced motion.

Natural motion has rest as its origin. A body moves only when it leaves its natural place and center, so it moves to return to it. Its departure from its center and place of rest is only by the moving of a compelling mover, so it has a forced motion that moves by the motion of the one who moves and compels it, and it has a natural motion by which it seeks, by its own nature, to return to its center. Both of its motions follow the compelling mover, so he is the origin of both motions.

Voluntary, willed motion is the origin of the other two, and it follows will and love.

The evidence that motions are confined to these three is this: if the moving thing has awareness of the motion, it is voluntary. If it has no awareness of it, then either it is in accordance with its nature or it is not. The first is natural, and the second is forced. Having established this, what exists in the heavens and the earth and between them, such as the motions of the spheres, the sun, the moon, the stars, the winds, the clouds, the rain, the plants, and the motions of embryos in their mothers' wombs, is only through the intermediary of the angels, who manage by command and distribute by command, as the texts of the Qur'an and the Sunnah indicate in many places.

Belief in this is part of the completeness of belief in the angels. Allah has entrusted the womb to angels, the rain to angels, the plants to angels, the winds to angels, and the spheres, the sun, the moon, and the stars. He has entrusted to every servant four angels: two recording angels, one on his right and one on his left, and two guardians, one before him and one behind him. He has entrusted angels with taking his soul and bringing it to its final abode in Paradise or the Fire, and angels with questioning and testing him in his grave, and angels with punishing him in the Fire or granting him bliss in Paradise. He has entrusted angels to the mountains, and angels to the clouds that drive them wherever they are commanded, and angels to the rain that descend by Allah's command in a known measure as Allah wills. He has entrusted angels with planting Paradise, working its vessels and furnishings, and tending it, and likewise angels with the Fire.

The greatest of Allah's hosts are the angels. The word malak (angel) suggests that he is a messenger who executes what another has commanded, and they have no share in the command at all. Rather, all the command belongs to Allah, and they manage the affair and distribute it by Allah's command and permission. Allah, exalted is He, said, reporting about them: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord. To Him belongs what is before us, what is behind us, and what is between that. And your Lord is not forgetful.﴾ [Maryam: 64].

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And how many an angel is there in the heavens whose intercession will avail nothing except after Allah gives permission to whom He wills and approves.﴾ [al-Najm: 26].

And He, glory be to Him, swore by groups of angels who execute His command in the creation, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿By those [ranks] lined up in rows, then those who drive [the clouds] with a driving, then those who recite the remembrance.﴾ [al-Saffat: 1–3].

And He said: ﴿By those sent forth in gusts, then those [winds] that blow violently, and those that spread [clouds] spreading, then those that separate, separating, then those that deliver a reminder, as an excuse or a warning.﴾ [al-Mursalat: 1–6].

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿By those who drag out [souls] with violence, and those who take [them] gently, and those who glide swiftly, then those who race ahead, then those who manage the affair.﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 1–5].

We have mentioned the meaning of this and the secret of swearing by it in the book (al-Tibyan fi Aqsam al-Qur'an, The Clarification of the Oaths of the Qur'an).

Once you know this, all those loves, movers, wills, and actions are an act of worship from them to the Lord of the earth and the heavens, and all natural and forced motions follow them. Were it not for love, the spheres would not revolve, the shining stars would not move, the subjugated winds would not blow, the carrying clouds would not pass, the embryos would not move in their mothers' wombs, the varieties of plants would not split forth from the seed, the surging waves would not churn, the managing and distributing [angels] would not move, and the earths and heavens would not glorify the One who originated them, nor would the varieties of creation within them. Glory be to the One: ﴿The seven heavens and the earth and whoever is in them glorify Him. And there is not a thing except that it glorifies Him by His praise, but you do not understand their glorification. Indeed, He is ever Forbearing and Forgiving.﴾ [al-Isra': 44].

[Section: Love for Allah Alone]

Having understood this, every living thing has will, love, and action according to its nature, and every moving thing has love and will as the origin of its motion. Existing things have no rectification except that their motions and their love be directed to their Originator and Creator alone, just as they have no existence except through His bringing them into being alone.

For this reason He, exalted is He, said: ﴿If there were in them gods other than Allah, they would both be ruined.﴾ [al-Anbiya': 22].

He, glory be to Him, did not say, "They would not have come into existence and would be non-existent," nor "They would be annihilated," because He is able to keep them in a state of corruption. But it is impossible for them to be in a state of rectification and uprightness except by His being the sole object of worship for both of them and for what they contain and what dwells in them. If there were two gods in the world, its order would be corrupted to the utmost extent, since each god would seek to overpower the other, to be exalted over him, and to be singled out from him in divinity, for partnership is a deficiency in the perfection of divinity, and a god does not accept for himself to be an imperfect god. If one of them overpowers the other, then he alone is God, and the one overpowered is not a god. If neither overpowers the other, then each is deficient and not perfect in divinity. Therefore there must be above both of them a god who subdues them and rules over them. Otherwise each would go off with what he created, and each would seek to be exalted over the other, and in that is the corruption of the affair of the heavens and the earth and of whoever is in them, just as is known of the corruption of a land when it has two equal kings, of a wife when she has two husbands, and of a she-camel when it has two stallions.

The root of the corruption of the world lies only in the disagreement of kings and caliphs. For this reason the enemies of Islam never hoped to attack it in any age except in an age when Muslim kings multiplied and disagreed, each of them became independent with a land, and some of them sought to be exalted over others.

Thus, the rectification of the heavens and the earth, their uprightness, and the orderly arrangement of creation in the most perfect order are among the clearest proofs that there is no god but Allah alone, with no partner. To Him belongs the dominion, and to Him belongs praise; He gives life and causes death, and He is powerful over all things. And every object of worship, from beneath His Throne down to the depths of the earth, is false, except His Supreme Face. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah has not taken any son, and there is not with Him any god. Otherwise, each god would have taken away what he created, and some of them would have exalted themselves over others. Glory be to Allah above what they describe. [He is] Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, so exalted is He above what they associate.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 91–93].

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Or have they taken gods from the earth who raise the dead? If there were in them gods other than Allah, they would both be ruined. So glory be to Allah, Lord of the Throne, above what they describe. He is not questioned about what He does, but they are questioned.﴾ [al-Anbiya': 21–23].

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: If there were with Him other gods, as they say, they would have sought a way to the Owner of the Throne.﴾ [al-Isra': 42].

It has been said: they would have sought a way to Him through overpowering and subduing, as kings do with one another. This is indicated by His saying in the other verse: ﴿and some of them would have exalted themselves over others.﴾

Our shaykh, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The correct meaning is: they would have sought a way to Him through drawing near to Him and obeying Him. How, then, do you worship them besides Him, when if they were gods as they claim, they would be servants of His? He said: There are several proofs for this:

Among them is His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Those whom they invoke seek means of access to their Lord, [striving as to] which of them would be nearest, hoping for His mercy and fearing His punishment.﴾ [al-Isra': 57].

That is: those whom you worship besides Me are My servants, just as you are My servants. They hope for My mercy and fear My punishment. So why do you worship them besides Me?

The second: He, glory be to Him, did not say "they would have sought [a way] over Him," but said "they would have sought a way to Him," and this expression is used only for drawing near, as in His saying: ﴿Fear Allah and seek the means to Him.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 35].

As for overpowering, it is used with "over," as in His saying: ﴿And if they obey you, do not seek a way against them.﴾ [al-Nisa': 34].

The third: they did not say that their gods overpower Him and seek to be exalted over Him. He, glory be to Him, has said: ﴿Say: If there were with Him gods, as they say.﴾ They were only saying that their gods seek to draw near to Him and bring them near to Him in nearness. So He said: If the matter were as you say, those gods would be servants of His. Then why do you worship His servants besides Him?

Natural motion has rest as its origin. A body moves only when it leaves its natural place and center, so it moves to return to it. Its departure from its center and place of rest is only by the moving of a compelling mover, so it has a forced motion that moves by the motion of the one who moves and compels it, and it has a natural motion by which it seeks, by its own nature, to return to its center. Both of its motions follow the compelling mover, so he is the origin of both motions.

Voluntary, willed motion is the origin of the other two, and it follows will and love.

The evidence that motions are confined to these three is this: if the moving thing has awareness of the motion, it is voluntary. If it has no awareness of it, then either it is in accordance with its nature or it is not. The first is natural, and the second is forced. Having established this, what exists in the heavens and the earth and between them, such as the motions of the spheres, the sun, the moon, the stars, the winds, the clouds, the rain, the plants, and the motions of embryos in their mothers' wombs, is only through the intermediary of the angels, who manage by command and distribute by command, as the texts of the Qur'an and the Sunnah indicate in many places.

Belief in this is part of the completeness of belief in the angels. Allah has entrusted the womb to angels, the rain to angels, the plants to angels, the winds to angels, and the spheres, the sun, the moon, and the stars. He has entrusted to every servant four angels: two recording angels, one on his right and one on his left, and two guardians, one before him and one behind him. He has entrusted angels with taking his soul and bringing it to its final abode in Paradise or the Fire, and angels with questioning and testing him in his grave, and angels with punishing him in the Fire or granting him bliss in Paradise. He has entrusted angels to the mountains, and angels to the clouds that drive them wherever they are commanded, and angels to the rain that descend by Allah's command in a known measure as Allah wills. He has entrusted angels with planting Paradise, working its vessels and furnishings, and tending it, and likewise angels with the Fire.

The greatest of Allah's hosts are the angels. The word malak (angel) suggests that he is a messenger who executes what another has commanded, and they have no share in the command at all. Rather, all the command belongs to Allah, and they manage the affair and distribute it by Allah's command and permission. Allah, exalted is He, said, reporting about them: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord. To Him belongs what is before us, what is behind us, and what is between that. And your Lord is not forgetful.﴾ [Maryam: 64].

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And how many an angel is there in the heavens whose intercession will avail nothing except after Allah gives permission to whom He wills and approves.﴾ [al-Najm: 26].

And He, glory be to Him, swore by groups of angels who execute His command in the creation, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿By those [ranks] lined up in rows, then those who drive [the clouds] with a driving, then those who recite the remembrance.﴾ [al-Saffat: 1–3].

And He said: ﴿By those sent forth in gusts, then those [winds] that blow violently, and those that spread [clouds] spreading, then those that separate, separating, then those that deliver a reminder, as an excuse or a warning.﴾ [al-Mursalat: 1–6].

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿By those who drag out [souls] with violence, and those who take [them] gently, and those who glide swiftly, then those who race ahead, then those who manage the affair.﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 1–5].

We have mentioned the meaning of this and the secret of swearing by it in the book (al-Tibyan fi Aqsam al-Qur'an, The Clarification of the Oaths of the Qur'an).

Once you know this, all those loves, movers, wills, and actions are an act of worship from them to the Lord of the earth and the heavens, and all natural and forced motions follow them. Were it not for love, the spheres would not revolve, the shining stars would not move, the subjugated winds would not blow, the carrying clouds would not pass, the embryos would not move in their mothers' wombs, the varieties of plants would not split forth from the seed, the surging waves would not churn, the managing and distributing [angels] would not move, and the earths and heavens would not glorify the One who originated them, nor would the varieties of creation within them. Glory be to the One: ﴿The seven heavens and the earth and whoever is in them glorify Him. And there is not a thing except that it glorifies Him by His praise, but you do not understand their glorification. Indeed, He is ever Forbearing and Forgiving.﴾ [al-Isra': 44].

[Section: Love for Allah Alone]

Having understood this, every living thing has will, love, and action according to its nature, and every moving thing has love and will as the origin of its motion. Existing things have no rectification except that their motions and their love be directed to their Originator and Creator alone, just as they have no existence except through His bringing them into being alone.

For this reason He, exalted is He, said: ﴿If there were in them gods other than Allah, they would both be ruined.﴾ [al-Anbiya': 22].

He, glory be to Him, did not say, "They would not have come into existence and would be non-existent," nor "They would be annihilated," because He is able to keep them in a state of corruption. But it is impossible for them to be in a state of rectification and uprightness except by His being the sole object of worship for both of them and for what they contain and what dwells in them. If there were two gods in the world, its order would be corrupted to the utmost extent, since each god would seek to overpower the other, to be exalted over him, and to be singled out from him in divinity, for partnership is a deficiency in the perfection of divinity, and a god does not accept for himself to be an imperfect god. If one of them overpowers the other, then he alone is God, and the one overpowered is not a god. If neither overpowers the other, then each is deficient and not perfect in divinity. Therefore there must be above both of them a god who subdues them and rules over them. Otherwise each would go off with what he created, and each would seek to be exalted over the other, and in that is the corruption of the affair of the heavens and the earth and of whoever is in them, just as is known of the corruption of a land when it has two equal kings, of a wife when she has two husbands, and of a she-camel when it has two stallions.

The root of the corruption of the world lies only in the disagreement of kings and caliphs. For this reason the enemies of Islam never hoped to attack it in any age except in an age when Muslim kings multiplied and disagreed, each of them became independent with a land, and some of them sought to be exalted over others.

Thus, the rectification of the heavens and the earth, their uprightness, and the orderly arrangement of creation in the most perfect order are among the clearest proofs that there is no god but Allah alone, with no partner. To Him belongs the dominion, and to Him belongs praise; He gives life and causes death, and He is powerful over all things. And every object of worship, from beneath His Throne down to the depths of the earth, is false, except His Supreme Face. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah has not taken any son, and there is not with Him any god. Otherwise, each god would have taken away what he created, and some of them would have exalted themselves over others. Glory be to Allah above what they describe. [He is] Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, so exalted is He above what they associate.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 91–93].

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Or have they taken gods from the earth who raise the dead? If there were in them gods other than Allah, they would both be ruined. So glory be to Allah, Lord of the Throne, above what they describe. He is not questioned about what He does, but they are questioned.﴾ [al-Anbiya': 21–23].

And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: If there were with Him other gods, as they say, they would have sought a way to the Owner of the Throne.﴾ [al-Isra': 42].

It has been said: they would have sought a way to Him through overpowering and subduing, as kings do with one another. This is indicated by His saying in the other verse: ﴿and some of them would have exalted themselves over others.﴾

Our shaykh, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The correct meaning is: they would have sought a way to Him through drawing near to Him and obeying Him. How, then, do you worship them besides Him, when if they were gods as they claim, they would be servants of His? He said: There are several proofs for this:

Among them is His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Those whom they invoke seek means of access to their Lord, [striving as to] which of them would be nearest, hoping for His mercy and fearing His punishment.﴾ [al-Isra': 57].

That is: those whom you worship besides Me are My servants, just as you are My servants. They hope for My mercy and fear My punishment. So why do you worship them besides Me?

The second: He, glory be to Him, did not say "they would have sought [a way] over Him," but said "they would have sought a way to Him," and this expression is used only for drawing near, as in His saying: ﴿Fear Allah and seek the means to Him.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 35].

As for overpowering, it is used with "over," as in His saying: ﴿And if they obey you, do not seek a way against them.﴾ [al-Nisa': 34].

The third: they did not say that their gods overpower Him and seek to be exalted over Him. He, glory be to Him, has said: ﴿Say: If there were with Him gods, as they say.﴾ They were only saying that their gods seek to draw near to Him and bring them near to Him in nearness. So He said: If the matter were as you say, those gods would be servants of His. Then why do you worship His servants besides Him?

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 21, verses 21–23:

Just as the heavens and the earth would be ruined if there were in them gods other than Him, glory be to Him, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿If there were in them gods other than Allah, they would both be ruined.﴾

Likewise, when the heart contains an object of worship other than Allah, exalted is He, it becomes corrupt with a corruption whose rectification is not hoped for, unless that object of worship is removed from the heart, and Allah alone becomes its god and its object of worship, the one it loves, hopes in, fears, relies upon, and turns to in repentance.

(Benefit)

Know that the subsistence of the heavens, the earth, and creation lies in their worship of the true God. If there were in them another god besides Allah, he would not be a true god, for the true God has no partner, no equal, and no like. If they were to worship other than Him, they would be utterly corrupted, since the cause of their rectification would be absent. Their rectification lies in the worship of the true God, just as they could not exist except by depending upon the one Lord, the Subduer. It is impossible for them to depend for their existence on two equal lords, and likewise it is impossible for them to depend for their continuance and rectification on two equal gods.

Having understood this, know that the servant's need to worship Allah alone, associating nothing with Him in love, fear, hope, reliance, action performed for Him, swearing by Him, vowing to Him, submission to Him, humbling oneself before Him, glorifying Him, prostrating to Him, and drawing near to Him, is greater than the body's need for its spirit and the eye's need for its light. Indeed, this need has no parallel by which it can be measured. The true reality of the servant is his spirit and his heart, and they have no rectification except through their God, besides whom there is no god. They find rest in this world only through His remembrance, and they are toiling toward Him with toil, so they will meet Him, and they must meet Him. They have no rectification except through loving Him, worshipping Him, His pleasure in them, and His honoring them. Even if the servant were to obtain from other than Allah all the pleasures and joys he could obtain, they would not last for him.

Rather, he moves from one kind to another and from one person to another. He enjoys something at one time and then is tormented by it at another time, without fail. Very often the thing he enjoys and takes pleasure in is not one that benefits him or gives him pleasure. It may even harm him to be connected to it and to have it near him, and it damages him. What he obtains through contact with it is of the same kind as what the mangy camel obtains from the pleasure of the nails that scratch it: they draw blood, tear the skin, and increase its harm, yet it prefers that because of the pleasure it finds in scratching. Likewise, what the heart suffers from the love of other than Allah is a torment upon it, a harm, and in reality a pain, whose pleasure does not exceed the pleasure of scratching the mange. The intelligent person weighs the two matters and prefers the weightier and more beneficial of them. Allah is the Granter of success and the Helper, and His is the conclusive proof, as He has the abundant blessing.

The point is that the god of the servant, whom he cannot do without at every state, every moment, and every blink of an eye, is the true God, and everything other than Him is false. He is wherever the servant is, and the servant's dependence on Him and need for Him cannot be compared to any dependence or need. Rather, it is above every dependence and greater than every need. For this reason the leader of the ḥanīfs (the monotheists who turned away from false worship) said: ﴿I do not love those that set.﴾ [al-An'am: 76]. And Allah knows best.

(Benefit)

Consider how the verse was brought in denouncing those who take, besides Him, gods that do not equal Him, and yet they equate them with Him despite the greatest difference.

His saying ﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾ establishes the reality of divinity and singles Him out for lordship and divinity.

His saying ﴿but they are questioned﴾ refers to the state of those gods taken as deities: they are questioned, they are lorded over, and they are managed.

How, then, can they be equated with Him despite the greatest distinction?

This is the matter the speech was brought to address. The Jabriyyah (a determinist sect that denies human agency) took them as a refuge and a stronghold in denying His wisdom and in explaining His acts by their praiseworthy purposes and their sound outcomes.

And Allah is the Granter of success in what is right.

The intercession that Allah has nullified is the intercession of a partner, for He has no partner. Therefore, the most fortunate of people in His intercession on the Day of Resurrection, the chief of the intercessors, are the people of tawhid (monotheism), who stripped tawhid bare and purified it from the attachments and impurities of shirk, and they are the ones with whom Allah is pleased.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And they do not intercede except for those whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya’: 28], and He says: ﴿On that Day, intercession will not benefit except for one whom the Most Merciful has permitted and whose word He has approved﴾ [Ta-Ha: 109].

So He informs that on that Day no intercession that benefits will occur except after the approval of the statement of the one for whom intercession is made, and His permission to the intercessor concerning him. As for the polytheist, He does not approve of him, nor is his word approved, so He does not permit the intercessors to intercede for him. For He, glory be to Him, has tied intercession to two matters:

His approval of the one for whom intercession is made, and His permission to the intercessor. So as long as the totality of the two matters does not exist, intercession does not exist.

The secret of this is that Allah alone possesses the whole command, so no one has any share of the command along with Him. The highest, most excellent and most honored of creation in His sight are the messengers and the angels brought near, and they are pure servants: they do not precede Him in speech, they do not step forward before Him, and they do nothing except after His permission and command to them. Especially on the Day when no soul will possess anything for another soul, they are owned and nurtured beings, whose actions are bound by His command and permission. So when the polytheist associates them with Allah and takes them as intercessors besides Him, supposing that by doing so they will step forward and intercede for him with Allah, he is among the most ignorant of people regarding the right of the Lord, what is due to Him, and what is impossible for Him. For this is an impossible, unthinkable notion, resembling the analogy of the Lord, the Exalted, to kings and great men, where a man takes from their close associates and allies someone who intercedes for him with them concerning his needs.

By this corrupt analogy the idols were worshipped, and the polytheists took intercessors and protectors besides Allah.

The difference between the two is the difference between the created and the Creator, the Lord and the one nurtured, the master and the servant, the owner and the owned, the self-sufficient and the poor, the One who has no need of anyone at all, and the one who is in need of another in every respect.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 21, verse 35:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We test you with evil and with good as a trial, and to Us you will be returned.﴾

Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said: "With hardship and ease, health and sickness, wealth and poverty, the lawful and the unlawful; and all of them are trials (balaʾ)."

Ibn Yazid said: "We test you with what you love and what you dislike, to see how you endure and how you give thanks, in what you love and what you dislike." Al-Kalbi said: "With evil: with poverty and affliction; and with good: with wealth and children." So He, glorified is He, informed that wealth and poverty are both vehicles (maṭiyya) of trial and examination.

If it is said: Iblis is pure evil, and disbelief and polytheism are likewise; yet they have come into existence. So what good is there in Iblis and in the existence of disbelief?

It is said: In the creation of Iblis there are wisdoms and benefits and goods that follow from his existence, which none knows but Allah, as we will point out some of them. Allah, glorified is He, did not create him in vain, nor did He intend by his creation the harm and destruction of His servants. How many a dazzling wisdom, overwhelming proof, manifest sign and abundant blessing there is in His creation. He, though he is for religions and faith like poisons for bodies, yet in the existence of poisons there are benefits and wisdoms that are better than their absence.

As for that which contains neither good nor evil, it does not enter existence either, for it would be in vain, and Allah is exalted above that. When the existence of this category is impossible, then the entry into existence of that in which evil outweighs good is even more deserving of being impossible. Whoever reflects on this existence knows that good predominates in it: illnesses, though many, are outnumbered by health; pleasures outnumber pains; well-being is greater than affliction; drowning, burning, collapse and the like, though many, are outweighed by safety. Had this category, whose good predominates, not existed because of the evil that occurs in it, the predominant good would have been lost, and the loss of predominant good is a predominant evil. An example of this is fire: in its existence there are many benefits, and in it there are harms; but when we compare its benefits with its harms, its harms have no proportion to its benefits. Likewise rain, winds, heat and cold. In sum, the elements of this lower world have their good mixed with their evil, but their good predominates; whereas the higher world is free of that.

(Section)

Among the signs of happiness and success is that the servant, whenever his knowledge increases, his humility and mercy increase; whenever his deeds increase, his fear and caution increase; whenever his life is extended, his greed decreases; whenever his wealth increases, his generosity and giving increase; and whenever his rank and standing increase, his nearness to people, his fulfilling of their needs, and his humility toward them increase.

And among the signs of wretchedness is that whenever his knowledge increases, his arrogance and conceit increase; whenever his deeds increase, his boasting, his contempt for people and his good opinion of himself increase; whenever his life is extended, his greed increases; whenever his wealth increases, his stinginess and withholding increase; and whenever his rank and standing increase, his arrogance and conceit increase.

These matters are a trial and examination from Allah, with which He tests His servants: by them some people are made happy and by them some people are made wretched. Likewise, honours are a trial and affliction, like kingship, authority and wealth. Allah, exalted is He, said concerning His Prophet Sulayman, when he saw the throne of Bilqis beside him: ﴿This is of the bounty of my Lord, to test me whether I will be grateful or ungrateful.﴾

So blessings are a trial from Allah, through which the gratitude of the grateful and the ingratitude of the ungrateful become apparent, just as afflictions are a test from Him, glorified is He. He tests with blessings just as He tests with calamities. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿As for man, when his Lord tests him by honouring him and bestowing blessings upon him, he says, "My Lord has honoured me." But when He tests him by restricting his provision, he says, "My Lord has humiliated me." No!﴾

That is: not everyone to whom You expand provision and honour and bless, it is an honouring from Me to him; and not everyone whose provision I restrict and whom I afflict, it is a humiliation from Me to him.

(Admonition)

People in this abode are all on a journey, and every traveller is heading toward his destination and descending upon one whose arrival delights him. The seeker of Allah and the Final Abode is, in truth, journeying toward Allah during his travel, and descending upon Him at the moment of arrival. This is his aspiration in his journey and at its end: ﴿O soul at peace, return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing. Enter among My servants, and enter My Paradise.﴾ And the wife of Pharaoh said: ﴿My Lord, build for me a house with You in Paradise.﴾ So she sought the house's being with Him before she sought it being in Paradise, for the neighbour comes before the house.

From the words of Shaykh ʿAli:

It was said to me in a sleep like wakefulness, or a wakefulness like sleep: "Do not show need to other than Me, lest I multiply it upon you as a recompense for your going beyond your limit in servitude.

I tested you with poverty so that you would become pure gold; so do not become counterfeit after the smelting.

I decreed poverty for you, and richness for Myself; if you join it to Me, I join you to richness, and if you join it to other than Me, I cut off the supplies of My aid from you, driving you away from My door.

Do not incline to anything apart from Us, for it is a calamity upon you and a killer of you.

If you incline to deeds, We return them to you; if you incline to gnosis, We make it unfamiliar to you; if you incline to ecstasy, We lead you astray within it; if you incline to knowledge, We stop you with it; if you incline to created beings, We leave you to them. Be pleased with Us as a Lord for you, and We will be pleased with you as a servant for Us."

Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 21, verse 42:

No one is more bountiful than Allah, the Glorified. His favour upon His servant is present in every breath and every moment, and the servant lives immersed in His favour in all his states. The servant has no way to count the kinds of this favour, let alone its types or individual instances. It is enough to note that among its kinds is the blessing of breath, which hardly crosses the servant's mind. In every day and night he has twenty-four thousand blessings from Him, for he breathes twenty-four thousand breaths in a day and a night, and every breath is a blessing from Allah, the Glorified. If the least of His blessings upon him in each day is twenty-four thousand blessings, what then is to be thought of what is above that and greater than it? ﴿And if you were to count the favour of Allah, you could not enumerate it﴾.

Added to this is what He averts from him of harms and kinds of harm that aim at him. Perhaps these balance the blessings in their abundance, and the servant is not aware of most of them at all. Allah, the Glorified, protects him from them by night and by day, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say: "Who protects you by night and by day from the Most Merciful?"﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:42]. Whether the meaning is "Who protects you and guards you from Him if He intends evil for you," with "yakla'uka" implying "yujirukum" (grants you refuge) and "yunajjikum" (saves you) from His punishment, or whether "min" is substitutive (badaliyya), meaning "Who protects you in place of the Most Merciful," that is, He alone is the one who protects you, and there is no protector for you other than Him, both readings are valid.

A parallel to this "min" is His saying: ﴿And if We willed, We would make angels from among you (min-kum) upon the earth, succeeding one another﴾ [al-Zukhruf 43:60], according to one of the two opinions, meaning "in your place and as your substitutes." They cited as evidence the verse of the poet:

*A maiden who had never eaten thin bread,*
*nor tasted pistachio among the herbs.*

That is, she had never eaten pistachio in place of herbs.

On both readings, He, the Glorified, bestows His favour upon them by protecting them, guarding them and watching over them from what harms them by night and by day, and He alone, with no guardian for them other than Him. This is in addition to His complete independence from them and their complete dependence on Him in every respect.

In some narrations Allah, the Exalted, says:

"I am the Generous. Who is more generous and bountiful than Me? I watch over My servants in their beds, while they challenge Me with great sins."

In al-Tirmidhi, the Prophet (ﷺ), when he saw the clouds, said:

"These are the water-carriers of the earth, which Allah drives toward a people who do not remember Him and do not worship Him."

In the two Sahih collections (Bukhari and Muslim), from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "No one is more patient with hearing harm than Allah. They attribute a son to Him, yet He provides for them and grants them well-being."

In some narrations: "Allah says: 'Son of Adam, My good comes down to you, and your evil ascends to Me. I draw near to you with blessings while I am independent of you, and you incite Me with sins while you are poor in need of Me. The noble angel will not cease to ascend to Me with an evil deed from you.'"

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 21, verse 47:

His saying: ﴿And We will set up the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection﴾. The lam (lam al-ta'lil, the lam of causation or purpose) may be the lam of causation, meaning: for the sake of the Day of Resurrection.

It has also been said that al-qist (justice) is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu, the object indicating the reason for an action), meaning: We set them up for the sake of justice, and it has fulfilled the conditions for its being in the accusative.

[Section: The Station of Ishfaq (Apprehensive Reverence)]

The heart in its journey to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is like a bird: love is its head, and fear and hope are its two wings. Whenever the head and the two wings are sound, the bird flies well. Whenever the head is cut off, the bird dies; and whenever the two wings are lost, it becomes easy prey for every hunter and predator. However, the early generations (al-salaf) preferred that in health the wing of fear should be stronger than the wing of hope, and at the time of departing from this world the wing of hope should become stronger than the wing of fear. This is the approach of Abu Sulayman and others. He said: "The heart should be dominated by fear; if hope dominates it, it is corrupted."

Another said: "The most perfect state is the balance of hope and fear, together with the dominance of love. Love is the vehicle; hope is the driver calling out; and fear is the one who drives on; and Allah is the One who brings (the traveller) to the destination by His favour and generosity."

[Section]

Among the stations of "You alone do we worship, and You alone do we ask for help" (Qur'an 1:5) is the station of ishfaq (apprehensive reverence).

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Those who fear their Lord unseen, and they are apprehensive of the Hour﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:49]. And He the Exalted said: ﴿And they will turn to one another, questioning. They will say: "Indeed, we were before this among our people apprehensive. So Allah has favoured us and protected us from the punishment of the scorching wind"﴾ [al-Tur 52:25-27].

Ishfaq is the tenderness of fear. It is a fear accompanied by compassion from the one who fears for the one about whom he fears. Its relation to fear is the relation of ra'fa (gentleness) to rahma (mercy), for it is the most delicate and tender form of mercy. For this reason the author of Manazil al-Sa'irin said:

"Ishfaq is the constant presence of caution, combined with compassion. It has three levels. The first: apprehensive concern for the self, lest it rush headlong into rebellion (ina'd), that is, hasten and go off along the path of desire and disobedience, and oppose servanthood."

"And apprehensive concern for the deed: that it should come to nothing (al-day'a)." That is, one fears for one's deed that it may be among those deeds of which Allah said: ﴿And We will turn to the works they did and make them scattered dust﴾ [al-Furqan 25:23]. These are the deeds done for other than Allah and not in accordance with His command and the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ). One also fears that one's deed may be lost in the future, either by abandoning it, or by sins that scatter and nullify it, so that it goes to waste, and the condition of its doer becomes like that of which Allah the Exalted spoke: ﴿Would any of you wish to have a garden of palm trees and grapevines, with rivers flowing beneath it, and for him therein every kind of fruit?﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:266], and so on.

'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) said to the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them): "Concerning whom do you think this verse was revealed?" They said: "Allah knows best." 'Umar became angry and said: "Say: 'We know,' or 'We do not know.'" Ibn 'Abbas said: "There is something in my heart about it, O Commander of the Faithful." He said: "O son of my brother, speak, and do not belittle yourself." Ibn 'Abbas said: "It was struck as a parable for a deed." 'Umar said: "What deed?" Ibn 'Abbas said: "For a deed." 'Umar said: "It is for a rich man who works in obedience to Allah; then Allah sends Satan to him, and he works at sins until he has drowned all his deeds."

He said: "And ishfaq toward creation, by knowing their excuses."

This may seem to involve a kind of contradiction: how can one feel apprehension while knowing the excuse? But there is no contradiction, for ishfaq, as stated earlier, is fear combined with mercy. One is apprehensive for them on account of their opposition to the command and prohibition, together with a kind of mercy, by considering the operation of divine decree over them.

He said: "The second level: ishfaq concerning the time, lest it be mixed with dispersion (tafarruq)." That is, one guards one's time lest there mingle with it what diverts one from presence with Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

He said: "And concerning the heart, lest some obstacle press upon it." The obstacle that presses may be lethargy (fatra), or doubt (shubha), or desire (shahwa), or any cause that hinders the wayfarer.

He said: "And concerning certainty (yaqin), lest a cause enter it which is tranquillity (tuma'nina) in one to whose hand all causes belong. Whenever reliance on a cause and attachment to it enter one's certainty, and one becomes content with it, this damages one's certainty. The intention is not to cut off causes from being causes, and to turn away from them, for this is zandaqa (heresy), disbelief, and impossibility. The Messenger was a cause for the attainment of guidance and faith; righteous deeds are a cause for salvation and entry into Paradise; disbelief is a cause for entry into the Fire; and visible causes are causes for their effects. But what one should guard against is attaching one's certainty to a cause other than Allah, and not becoming attached to causes but rather passing away (fana') in the Causer, beyond them."

The Shaykh is among those who greatly exaggerate in denying causes; he sees no beyond the annihilation (fana') in the Tawhid of Lordship as an ultimate goal. His discourse in the third level, in most chapters, returns to these two principles. You have come to know what is in them, and that the correct view is the opposite of both: affirming causes and powers, and that annihilation in the Tawhid of Lordship is not the ultimate goal of the path, but that above it there is something greater, higher and more noble.

From these two foundations arose, in his book, some of the matters for which he was criticised.

He said: "The third level: ishfaq that guards one's striving from self-admiration ('ujb), restrains its possessor from quarrelling with people, and drives the aspirant to preserve earnestness (jidd)."

The first relates to the deed, the second to character, and the third to the will (irada), and each has something that corrupts it.

Self-admiration corrupts the deed just as showing off (riya') corrupts it, so one is apprehensive for one's striving from this corrupter, with an apprehension that guards one from it.

Quarrelling with people corrupts character, so one is apprehensive for one's character from this corrupter, with an apprehension that guards one from it.

The will is corrupted by the absence of earnestness, which is frivolity and play, so one is apprehensive for one's will from what corrupts it.

When one's deed, character and will are sound, one's conduct, heart and state are upright. And Allah is the One sought for help.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 21, verses 51–52:

His words, glorified is He: ﴿And We had certainly given Abraham his sound judgment before, and We were of him well-Knowing.﴾

The most correct view regarding the verse is that the meaning is "before the revelation of the Torah," for He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And We had certainly given Moses and Aaron the Criterion and a light and a reminder for the God-fearing.﴾ And He said: ﴿And this is a blessed reminder which We have sent down. So will you deny it?﴾ Then He said: ﴿And We had certainly given Abraham his sound judgment before,﴾ that is, before them. For this reason, (qabl) is cut off from being followed by a genitive and is built (on a vowel), because the omitted complement is understood, even though it is not mentioned in the wording.

And He, glorified is He, mentioned these three, and they are the leaders of the messengers and the most honored of creation before Him: Muhammad, Abraham, and Moses.

It has been said that (min qabl) means "in the state of his youth, before puberty," but there is nothing in the wording that indicates this context; rather it requires only "before what was mentioned."

It has also been said that the meaning of His words "from before" is "in what was already known to Us."

Nor is there anything in the verse indicating this, and it is not a matter specific to Abraham; rather, every believer—God has decreed his guidance in His foreknowledge.

The intended point is His words: ﴿and We were of him well-Knowing.﴾

Al-Baghawi said: "that he was fit for guidance and prophethood."

Abu al-Faraj said: "that is, knowing that he was a place for the bestowal of sound judgment."

The author of al-Kashshaf said: "The meaning is that His knowledge of him is that He knew from him wondrous conditions, marvelous secrets, and qualities with which He was pleased and which He praised, until He qualified him for His friendship and sincere intimacy. This is like your saying about a free man among people: 'I know so-and-so.'

So your words here encompass the excellence of descriptions."

This is like His saying: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ and His saying: ﴿And We chose them with knowledge over the worlds﴾. Its counterpart is His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah chose Adam, Noah, the family of Abraham, and the family of 'Imran over the worlds, descendants, one of another. And Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾

And close to it is His saying: ﴿And to Solomon the wind, blowing forcefully, running by his command toward the land which We had blessed. And We are ever, of all things, Knowing.﴾ Here We placed this specification in the place that befits it among places and people.

(Benefit)

Inābah (turning in repentance) is the heart's devotion to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, like the body's remaining in the mosque, never departing from it. Its reality is the heart's devotion to His love and remembrance with reverence and glorification, and the limbs' devotion to His obedience through sincerity toward Him and following His Messenger. Whoever's heart does not devote itself to Allah alone devotes itself to various images, as the Imam of the Hanifs said to his people: ﴿What are these images to which you are devoted?﴾

So he and his people divided the reality of devotion: the portion of his people was devotion to images, and his portion was devotion to the Majestic Lord. Images (tamathil) is the plural of timthal, which is the sculpted forms. So the heart's attachment to other than Allah, its preoccupation with it, and its inclination toward it is a devotion from it to the images that have settled in its heart. This is similar to devotion to idol-images, and for this reason the polytheism of idol-worshippers consisted of devotion with their hearts, aspirations, and wills toward their images. So if there are images in the heart that have taken possession of it and enslaved it, such that it is devoted to them, this is like the devotion of idols to them. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) called such a person a slave to them and invoked against him with ruin and reversal, saying: "Ruined is the slave of the dinar, ruined is the slave of the dirham, ruined and reversed; and if he is pricked, may he not be relieved."

When you say "a'fa'alta kadha" (did you do this?) and begin with the verb, the doubt lies in the act itself, and the purpose of the interrogative is your knowledge of whether it occurred. So there is a difference between your saying "a-kataba al-kitab?" (did you write the book?) and your saying "a-anta katabtahu?" (was it you who wrote it?).

(Lataifah)

I visited you out of longing, and even if the distance had spread
The desert's floor between us as embers, I would still have visited you.

The Friend (Khalil, i.e., Abraham) never travelled a journey, nor took a path, more pleasant than the wilderness he entered when he came out of the catapult's pan.

Gabriel saw him bidding farewell to the land of habit, so he assumed weakness in his reliance on God, and offered him provision, saying, "Do you have any need?" He refused with dignity, saying, "As for you, no."

When his fulfilment of what he was commanded was complete, his robe of honour came to him: ﴿And Abraham, who fulfilled [his covenant]﴾.

(Faidah)

On the authority of Qatadah, who said: I asked Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib about a woman who comes to her husband, and magic is undone for her, and he said: "There is no harm." I said to Ahmad: "Shall I narrate this from you?" He said: "Yes."

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 21, verse 78–79 (part 1 of 3):

Mention of the two noble Prophets, and praise of them for judgment and knowledge, and the specification of one of them with understanding the case.

(A benefit)

The judge (qadi) and the mufti (jurist who issues legal opinions) share the fact that each of them must make clear the ruling of the Sharia on the matter, but the judge is distinguished by enforcing it and executing it. Accordingly, the conditions for the judge return to the conditions of the witness, the mufti, and the governor: he reports the ruling of the Lawgiver by his knowledge, is accepted by his uprightness, and executes it by his power.

[Chapter: The judgment of the two noble Prophets, Dawud and Sulayman]

Al-harth (الحَرْث) is the orchard. It has been narrated that it was a vineyard, which is called al-karm. Al-nafsh (النَّفْش) is the grazing of sheep at night. Dawud judged by the value of what was destroyed, so he assessed the sheep and found them equal in value to the damage, and he handed them over to the owners of the field, either because they had no dirhams, or because selling them was impossible, and they agreed to take them in place of the value, and those (the owners of the sheep) agreed to hand them over as a substitute for the value.

As for Sulayman, he ruled that the owners of the sheep were liable and must compensate by the equivalent: by restoring the orchard until it returns as it was. He did not deprive them of the produce lost due to the destruction until the time of its return; rather, he gave the owners of the orchard the flock of those people so that they could take from its increase in proportion to the increase of the orchard, thus obtaining from the increase of their sheep the equivalent of what they had lost of the increase of their field. He considered the two increases and found them equal. This is the knowledge which Allah specified for him and praised him for grasping.

The scholars of the Muslims have disputed over such a case in four opinions:

The first: agreement with the Sulaymanic ruling regarding liability for the nafsh and regarding compensation by the equivalent. This is the truth. It is one of the two opinions in the school of Ahmad, and a view of the Shafi'is and Malikis, though the well-known position among them is otherwise.

The second opinion: agreement with him regarding liability for the nafsh, but not regarding compensation by the equivalent. This is the well-known position of the schools of Malik, al-Shafi'i and Ahmad.

The third: agreement with him regarding compensation by the equivalent, but not regarding the nafsh, as when its owner grazed it by his own choice, as opposed to when it strayed and he was unaware of it. This is the opinion of Dawud and those who agree with him.

The fourth opinion: that the nafsh does not create liability in any case, and what is due from the shepherd's liability other than for nafsh is compensated by value, not by equivalent. This is the school of Abu Hanifa.

What the Prophet of Allah Sulayman ruled is the closest to justice and analogy. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ruled that the owners of orchards must guard them by day, and that what livestock destroys at night is a liability on its owners. Thus by his ruling the liability for nafsh is established, and by the previous texts and sound analogy the liability by equivalent is established, and by the text of the Book the praise of Sulayman for understanding this ruling is established. So it is established that it is correct, and success is from Allah.

[Chapter: The level of understanding]

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Dawud and Sulayman, when they judged concerning the field when the sheep of a people grazed in it by night, and We were witnesses to their judgment. And We gave understanding of it to Sulayman, and to each We gave judgment and knowledge.﴾ [al-Anbiya: 78–79]

So He mentioned these two noble Prophets, praised them for knowledge and judgment, and specified Sulayman with understanding in this particular case. Ali ibn Abi Talib, when asked, "Did the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) specify you with anything apart from the people?" said: "No, by Him who split the grain and created the soul, except an understanding which Allah gives a servant in His Book, and what is in this document." And in it was the diya (blood money), the ransom of captives, and that a Muslim is not to be killed for a disbeliever.

In the letter of Umar ibn al-Khattab to Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, may Allah be pleased with both of them: "And understanding, understanding in what is presented to you." Understanding is a blessing from Allah upon His servant, and a light which Allah casts into his heart, by which he recognizes and perceives what others do not perceive or recognize, so he understands from the text what others do not understand, despite both being equal in memorizing it and in understanding its basic meaning.

Thus understanding from Allah and His Messenger is the sign of sincerity (siddiqiyya) and the banner of prophetic guardianship. In it the ranks of scholars vary, to the point that one is counted as a thousand. Consider the understanding of Ibn Abbas, when Umar asked him and those present from the people of Badr and others about the surah ﴿When the help of Allah comes and the victory﴾ [al-Nasr: 1], and what Ibn Abbas was specified with in understanding from it: that it is Allah's notification to His Prophet of his own death and informing him of the approach of his term, and Umar's agreement with him on that, and its being hidden from others of the Companions, though Ibn Abbas was the youngest of them in age at that time. Where would you find in this surah the announcement of his term, were it not for special understanding? This subtlety goes deep, reaching levels which the understanding of most people falls short of, so that with the text they need something else, and the text alone does not suffice for them; but for the one with understanding, he does not need anything beyond the texts.

[Chapter: Examples of judgment by insight and indicators]

Among judgment by insight and indicators is what Muhammad ibn Ubayd Allah ibn Abi Rafi' narrated from his father, who said: A young man from the Ansar brought a case against his mother to Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him. She denied him, so he asked him for evidence, but he had none. The woman brought a group who testified that she had not married and that the young man was lying about her, and that he had slandered her.

Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, ordered him to be flogged. Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, met him and asked about their matter, and he was informed. He summoned them, then sat in the mosque of the Prophet (ﷺ) and questioned the woman, and she denied it. He said to the young man: "Deny her as she denied you." He said: "O cousin of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), she is my mother." He said: "Deny her, and I am your father, and al-Hasan and al-Husayn are your brothers." He said: "I have denied her and rejected her."

Ali said to the guardians of the woman: "Is my decision regarding this woman permissible?" They said: "Yes, and it is also in our hands." Ali said: "I call upon those present to witness that I have married this young man to this woman, who is a stranger to him." "O Qanbar, bring me a pouch containing a dirham." He brought it, and he counted four hundred and eighty dirhams, and gave them to her as her dower.

He said to the young man: "Take the hand of your wife, and do not come to us except with the mark of the wedding upon you." When he turned away, the woman said: "O Abu al-Hasan, by Allah, the Fire! By Allah, he is my son."

He said: "How is that?" She said: "His father was a Zanji (African), and my brothers married me to him, and I conceived this boy. The man went out to fight and was killed, and I sent this boy to the clan of Bani Fulan. He grew up among them, and I was ashamed for him to be my son." Ali said: "I am Abu al-Hasan," and he attached him to her, and his lineage was established.

Among that also: Umar ibn al-Khattab asked a man: "How are you?" He said: "One who loves strife, hates the truth, and testifies to what he has not seen." So Umar ordered him to prison. Ali ordered his release, and said: "He has spoken truly." He said: "How did you judge him truthful?" He said: "He loves wealth and children."

Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿Your wealth and your children are only a trial﴾ [al-Taghabun: 15]. "He hates death, which is the truth. He testifies that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), though he has not seen him." So Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, ordered his release, and said: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am: 124].

Ja'far ibn Muhammad said: Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, was brought a woman who had become attached to a young man of the Ansar, and she loved him. When he did not comply with her, she schemed against him: she took an egg, broke it, discarded the yolk, and poured the white over her garment and between her thighs. Then she came to Umar crying out, saying: "This man overpowered me against my will, and disgraced me before my family, and this is the trace of his deed." Umar asked the women, and they said to him: "Indeed, there is on her body and garment a trace of semen." He resolved to punish the young man, and he began to plead, saying: "O Commander of the Faithful, reflect on my matter, for by Allah I did not commit an immoral act, nor did I intend it. She sought to seduce me, but I refrained." Umar said: "O Abu al-Hasan, what do you see regarding their matter?" Ali looked at what was on the garment. Then he called for water, very hot and boiling, and poured it on the garment, and that white substance congealed. He took it, smelled it and tasted it, and recognized the taste of egg white, and rebuked the woman, and she confessed.

I say: Similar to this is what al-Khiraqi and others narrated from Ahmad: that if a woman claims that her husband is impotent, and he denies it, and she is a non-virgin, then he is left alone with her in a room, and it is said to him: "Release your fluid onto something." If she claims that it is not semen, it is placed over fire; if it melts, it is semen, and her claim is refuted. This is the position of Ata ibn Abi Rabah. This is a judgment by apparent indicators, for semen when placed over fire melts and dissolves, whereas if it is egg white it congeals and dries. If he says, "I am unable to release my fluid," her claim is upheld.

Asbagh ibn Nubata said: A young man complained to Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, about a group of men, saying: "These people went out with my father on a journey. They returned, but my father did not return. I asked them about him, and they said: 'He died.' I asked them about his wealth, and they said: 'He left nothing,' though he had much wealth with him." We brought the matter to Shurayh, who made them swear oaths and released them. Ali then summoned the guards, assigned two men to each man, and instructed them not to allow any of them to approach another, nor to let anyone speak to them. He summoned his scribe, and summoned one of them.

He said: "Tell me about this young man's father: On what day did he go out with you? At what station did you halt? How was your journey? Of what illness did he die? How was his wealth taken? And who washed and buried him? Who led the prayer over him? And where was he buried?" and similar questions, while the scribe wrote. Then Ali said "Allahu akbar," and those present said it too, and the accused, who had no knowledge, assumed that their companion had confessed against them. Then he summoned another after removing the first from the assembly, and asked him as he had asked his companion, then the third likewise, until he knew what all had. He found that each one reported the opposite of what his companion had reported. Then he ordered the first to be brought back, and said: "O enemy of Allah, I have recognized your treachery and lying through what I heard from your companions, and nothing will save you from punishment except truthfulness." Then he ordered him to prison, and said "Allahu akbar," and those present said it with him. When the people saw the situation, they did not doubt that their companion had confessed against them. He summoned another of them and threatened him, and he said: "O Commander of the Faithful, by Allah, I was averse to what they did." Then he summoned all of them, and they confessed to the account. The one in prison was brought out, and it was said to him: "Your companions have confessed, and nothing will save you but truthfulness," so he confessed like the others. So he made them pay the wealth, and carried out retaliation against them for the killing.

A man was brought before one of the judges who had struck another man on the head. The one who was struck claimed that he had destroyed his sight and sense of smell. The judge said: "He is to be tested: he should raise his eyes to the disc of the sun. If he is sound, his eyes do not stay fixed upon it, and tears flow from them. A cloth is burned and brought to his nose. If his sense of smell is sound, the smell reaches his nasal passage and his eyes water."

I saw in "The Judgments of Ali, may Allah be pleased with him" a parallel to this case, in which the one who was struck claimed he was mute. He ordered that his tongue be brought out and pricked with a needle: if the blood that comes out is red, he is sound of tongue; if it comes out black, he is mute.

Asbagh ibn Nubata said: Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, was asked about the ransom of Muslim captives from the hands of the polytheists. He said: "Call out for those whose wounds are in front of them, not those whose wounds are behind them, for that one is a fleer."

Ali also judged in the case of a woman who married; on the night of her wedding she secretly admitted her lover into the bridal chamber. The husband came and entered the chamber, and the lover leapt at him and they fought, and the husband killed the lover. Then the woman stood up against him and killed him. Ali ruled the blood money of the lover against the woman, then he executed her for the husband. He ruled the blood money of the lover against her because she was the one who had exposed him to killing the husband; she was the cause of his death, and she was more deserving of liability than the husband who directly did it, because the one who directly did it killed him in a permitted manner, in defense of his honor. This is among the finest judgments, which many jurists do not arrive at, and it is the correct one.

And he (ʿUmar or the judge, as the text reports) ruled concerning a man who fled from another man who wanted to kill him, and a third man held him in place for him until he caught up and killed him. Nearby was a man who watched them both while he was able to rescue him, but he stood and watched until he was killed. So he ruled that the killer be executed, that the one who held him be imprisoned until he dies, and that the eye of the watcher who stood by and did not object be put out.

Amir al-Mu'minin ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, ruled concerning a man who cut off his wife's genitals: the full diyah (blood money) for the genitals is to be taken from him, and he is to be compelled to keep her until she dies. If he divorces her, he must still maintain her financially.

How excellent this judgment is, and how close it is to the truth! As for the genitals, the full diyah is due for them by consensus (ijma'). As for his maintaining her if he divorces her, that is because he has ruined her for the husbands who would have supported her and provided for her needs, a ruin that never returns. As for compelling him to keep her, it is a punishment for him with the opposite of his intent, for he intended to be rid of her by a forbidden means, while he could have been rid of her by talaq (divorce) or khul' (divorce initiated by the wife through compensation). Instead he turned away from that to this vile mutilation, so his recompense is to be bound to keeping her until death.

He also ruled concerning a newborn who had two heads and two chests on one torso. They asked him: Is he to inherit the inheritance of two people or of one? He said: Leave him until he sleeps, then call out to him. If both wake together, he has the inheritance of one; if one wakes and the other remains asleep, he has the inheritance of two.

Among such cases: ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, was brought a woman who had committed zina (unlawful intercourse). He questioned her and she confessed, so he ordered her stoned. ʿAli said: Perhaps she has an excuse. Then he said to her: What drove you to fornication? She said: I had a partner, and his camels had water and milk, while my camels had no water or milk. I became thirsty and asked him for a drink, but he refused to give me any until I gave him myself. I refused him three times. When I became very thirsty and thought my soul would leave me, I gave him what he wanted, and he gave me to drink. Then ʿAli said: Allahu Akbar! ﴿But whoever is compelled, neither desiring it nor exceeding the limit, there is no sin upon him. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 173].

Also among the judgments of ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him: a man was brought to him who had been found in a ruined house with a knife in his hand stained with blood, and before him was a slain man writhing in his blood. He questioned him, and he said: I killed him. ʿAli said: Take him and kill him. As he was being taken away, a man came running and said: O people, do not hurry! Bring him back to ʿAli. They brought him back, and the man said: O Amir al-Mu'minin, this is not his companion; I killed him. ʿAli said to the first man: What led you to say, "I am his killer," when you did not kill him? He said: O Amir al-Mu'minin, what could I do? The night watch (ʿasas) found the man writhing in his blood, while I was standing with a knife in my hand bearing traces of blood, and I had been seized in a ruined house. I feared that my word would not be accepted, and that this would be a qasamah (the oath procedure in cases of homicide), so I confessed to what I had not done, and I sought my reward with Allah.
