ʿAli said: What you did was wretched. So what was your account? He said: I am a butcher. I went out to my shop in the dawn darkness, slaughtered a cow, and skinned it. While I was skinning it with the knife in my hand, I needed to urinate. I came to a ruined house nearby, entered it, relieved myself, and then returned, intending to go to my shop. Suddenly I saw this slain man writhing in his blood, and his condition frightened me. I stood looking at him with the knife in my hand, and I did not realize anything until your companions had stood over me and seized me. The people said: This one killed this one, and there is no killer for him other than him. I became certain that you would not abandon their word for my word, so I confessed to what I had not committed.

ʿAli then said to the second confessor: And what was your story? He said: Iblis (Satan) led me astray. I killed the man out of greed for his wealth. Then I heard the sound of the night watch, so I came out of the ruined house and encountered this butcher in the state he described. I hid from him behind part of the ruin until the night watch came, seized him, and brought him to you. When you ordered his execution, I knew that I would bear his blood as well, so I confessed to the truth.

Then ʿAli said to al-Hasan: What is the ruling concerning him? Al-Hasan said: O Amir al-Mu'minin, if he killed a soul, he has given life to a soul, and Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿And whoever saves one, it is as if he had saved all of mankind﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 32]. So ʿAli released both of them and paid the diyah for the slain man from the public treasury (bayt al-mal).

Four women came before Iyas ibn Muʿawiyah. Iyas said: One of them is pregnant, another is nursing, another is a thayyib (previously married woman), and another is a virgin (bikr). They looked and found the matter just as he had said. They said: How did you know? He said: As for the pregnant one, she was speaking to me while lifting her garment from her belly, so I knew she was pregnant. As for the nursing one, she was striking her breast, so I knew she was nursing. As for the thayyib, she was speaking to me with her eyes meeting mine, so I knew she was a thayyib. As for the virgin, she was speaking to me with her eyes on the ground, so I knew she was a virgin.

Al-Mada'ini related from Rawh: A man from among the trustworthy people deposited money with a man. Later he returned and asked for his deposit, but the man denied it. So he went to Iyas and told him. Iyas said to him: Go away, keep your matter secret, and do not let him know that you came to me. Then return to me after two days. Iyas then summoned the depositary and said: A large amount of money has come, and I want to hand it over to you. Is your house spacious? He said: Yes. He said: Prepare a place for it and porters. The man returned to Iyas, and Iyas said: Go to your companion and ask for the money. If he gives it to you, well and good; if he denies you, say to him: I will inform the judge. So the man went to his companion and said: Give me my money, or I will go to the judge, complain to him, and inform him of my affair. So the man handed over his money. The depositary returned to Iyas and said: He has given me the money. When the trustee came to Iyas for his appointment, Iyas rebuked and scolded him, and said: Do not come near me, you traitor!

Yazid ibn Harun, may Allah have mercy on him, said: A trustworthy man was appointed in Wasit. A man deposited a sealed bag with one of his witnesses and mentioned that it contained a thousand dinars. When the owner's absence was prolonged, the witness opened the bag from its bottom, took the dinars, put dirhams in their place, and resewed it as it had been. Then the owner came, asked for his deposit, and the witness handed him the bag with its seal unchanged. When he opened it and saw the state of affairs, he returned to the witness and said: I deposited dinars with you, and what you gave me is dirhams. The witness said: It is your bag with your seal. So the owner sought the judge's help against him. The judge ordered the depositary to be brought. When they stood before him, the judge said: Since when did he deposit this bag with you? He said: Fifteen years ago. The judge took those dirhams and read their minting, and found that they had been struck two or three years earlier. So he ordered him to hand over the dinars to the owner, dismissed him from his post, and proclaimed his disgrace.

A man deposited money with another man, who denied it. The owner brought the matter to Iyas. Iyas asked him, and he denied it. Iyas said to the claimant: Where did you hand it over to him? He said: In a place in the desert. Iyas said: And what was there? He said: A tree. Iyas said: Go to it, perhaps you buried the money near it and forgot, and you will remember when you see the tree. So he went off. Iyas said to the opponent: Sit until your companion returns. Iyas continued judging, and every so often he looked at him. Then he said to him: Tell me, do you see that your companion has reached the place of the tree? He said: No. Iyas said: O enemy of Allah, you are a traitor! The man said: Forgive me! Iyas said: May Allah not forgive you. He ordered that he be held in custody until the man returned, and Iyas said to him: Go with him and take your right.

A similar case occurred with another judge: a man claimed before him that he had handed a debtor money as a deposit, and the debtor denied it. The judge said to him: Where did you hand it over to him? He said: In a mosque far from the town. The judge said: Go and bring me a copy of the Qur'an from it, so that I may make him swear upon it. The man went off. The judge detained the debtor and then said to him: Do you think he has reached the mosque yet? He said: No. So the judge held him liable for the money.

Judge Abu Hazim had, in such matters, remarkable wonders, and people would object to him, but then the truth would become clear in what he did.

Makram ibn Ahmad said: I was in the assembly of the judge Abu Hazim when an old man came forward with a young boy, and the old man claimed a debt of a thousand dinars against him. He said: What do you say? The boy said: Yes. The judge said to the old man: What do you want? He said: His imprisonment. The judge said: No. The old man said: If the judge sees fit to imprison him, it is more likely to secure my money. Abu Hazim studied them both for a while, then said: Remain bound to one another until I look into your matter at another session. I said to him: Why did you postpone his imprisonment? He said: Woe to you! In most situations I can recognize in the faces of litigants the face of the one who is right from the one who is wrong, and I have acquired a discernment in this that rarely errs. It has occurred to me that this young man's readiness to confess is a sign of his lying, and perhaps the matter will become clear to me so that I may proceed with insight. Do you not see how little these two investigate the denial, how little they dispute, and how calm their temperaments are despite the great amount of money? The habit of youths is not to be excessively scrupulous until someone like this confesses readily and quickly, with a content heart concerning this money. He said: While we were talking like this, the gatekeeper came asking permission to enter for one of the merchants. The judge allowed him. When he entered he said: May Allah set the judge right! I have been afflicted with a young son who squanders every bit of money he gets from me on singing girls with so-and-so. When I prevent him, he devises stratagems that force me to take on his debts. Today the owner of the singing girls has come forward, demanding a thousand dinars immediately, and I have heard that he has approached the judge to have him confess so that he can imprison him. And he is in trouble with his mother, which embitters our life until I settle his debts. When I heard of this, I hurried to the judge to explain his situation. The judge smiled and said to me: How did you see it? I said: This is from Allah's favor upon the judge. He said: Bring me the young man and the old man. Abu Hazim frightened the old man and admonished the young man. They confessed, and the man took his son and left.

Abu al-Sa'ib said: In our town there was a man of concealed condition (mastur al-hal), and the judge wished to accept his testimony. He inquired about him, and he was praised to him both privately and publicly. So the judge summoned him to attend the session to give testimony. The judge sat, and the man attended. When he came to give his testimony, the judge did not accept it. He was asked about the reason, and he said: It became clear to me that he is a hypocrite (murai), so I could not accept his word. He was asked: From where did you know that? He said: He used to come to me every day, and I would count his steps from the point where my eye first fell on him at the door until he reached my seat. When I summoned him today and he came, I counted his steps from that same point, and they had increased by three or about that. So I knew he was affecting something, and I did not accept him.

Ibn Qutaybah said: al-Farazdaq testified before some of the judges, and he said: We have accepted the testimony of Abu Firas and Zaydun. When he left, he was told: By Allah, he did not accept your testimony.

Allah's insight belongs to the one who is the imam of those who discern and the shaykh of those who read signs: ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, whose insight never erred, and who judged among the Ummah by insight supported by revelation.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 21, verse 78–79 (part 3 of 3):

Al-Layth ibn Sa'd said: One day, a beardless youth was brought to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who had been found slain, thrown on the side of the road. 'Umar inquired about his matter and made every effort, but he could not come upon any information about it, and this grieved him. So he said: "O Allah, grant me victory over his killer." Then, when a full year had passed, an infant was found, newly born, thrown at the place where the slain man had been. He was brought to 'Umar, who said: "By Allah's will, I have obtained retribution for the blood of the slain man." He gave the infant to a woman and said to her: "Look after him, take his maintenance from us, and watch who takes him from you. When you find a woman who kisses him and presses him to her breast, inform me of her whereabouts."

When the infant grew up, a slave girl came and said to the woman: "My mistress has sent me to you so that you may send the boy to her, so that she may see him and return him to you." The woman said: "Yes, go with him to her, and I will accompany you." So she went with the boy, the woman accompanying her, until they entered upon her mistress. When she saw him, she took him, kissed him and pressed him to her. Behold, she was the daughter of an old man from the Ansar, one of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The woman went to 'Umar and informed him. He girded on his sword and went to the woman's house. He found her father reclining at the door of his house, and he said to him: "O so-and-so, what has your daughter, so-and-so, done?"

He said: "May Allah reward her with good, O Commander of the Faithful. She is among the people most knowing of the right of Allah and the right of her father, along with her good prayer, her fasting, and her upholding of her religion." 'Umar said: "I wish to enter upon her, so that I may increase her desire for good and urge her toward it." So her father entered, and 'Umar entered with him. 'Umar ordered those with her to leave, and they departed, and he and the woman remained in the house. 'Umar uncovered the sword and said: "Be truthful with me, or I will strike off your neck," and he never lied. She said: "Be patient. By Allah, I will speak the truth: an old woman used to visit me, and I took her as a mother, and she would attend to my affairs as a mother does. I was to her like a daughter, until a period passed. Then she said: 'O my daughter, a journey has come up for me, and I have a daughter in a place where I fear she may be lost. I wish to entrust her to you until I return from my journey.' Then she took a son of hers, a young beardless youth, dressed him in the likeness of a girl, and brought him to me, and I had no doubt that he was a girl. So he would see from me what a girl sees from a girl, until one day he caught me unawares while I was asleep. I did not perceive until he had mounted me and penetrated me. I stretched my hand to a knife that was at my side, and I killed him."

Then I ordered that he be cast away wherever I saw fit, and I conceived this infant from him. When I gave birth, I cast him at the place of his father. This, by Allah, is their story as I have informed you." He said: "You have spoken the truth." Then he counselled her, prayed for her, and departed. He said to her father: "What an excellent daughter you have!" Then he left.

Among such instances is the insight (firasah) of Ibn 'Umar concerning al-Husayn when he bade him farewell and said: "I entrust you to Allah from being slain," while he had with him the letters of the people of Iraq. Ibn 'Umar's insight was more truthful than their letters.

Among such instances: two men from Quraysh deposited with a woman one hundred dinars as a trust, and said: "Do not hand it over to either of us without the other." They remained for a year, then one of them came and said: "My companion has died, so hand the dinars over to me." She refused and said: "You both told me, 'Do not hand it over to either of us without the other,' so I will not hand it over to you." She was pressed by her family and neighbours until she handed it over to him. Then she remained another year, and the other came and said: "Hand over the dinars to me." She said: "Your companion came to me and claimed that you had died, so I handed it over to him." They disputed before 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and he intended to rule against her. She said: "Refer us to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib." 'Ali realised that the two had deceived her, and said: "Did you not both say, 'Do not hand it over to either of us without the other'?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Then your property is with her. Go and bring your companion, so that she may hand it over to you both."

[Chapter: On the insight of the judge]

Among the insight of the judge is what Hammad ibn Salamah related from Humayd al-Tawil: that two men disputed before Iyas ibn Mu'awiyah, one of whom had deposited a trust with his companion. The owner of the trust said: "Make him swear by Allah that I have no trust with him." Iyas said: "Rather, I will make him swear by Allah that you have no trust with him, nor anything else."

This is among the finest insight, for if he says, "I have no trust with him," it admits of negation, and also of affirmation, since one may read "mala" as governed by a verb understood, meaning: he delivered his property to me, or gave me his property; or one may take "ma" as a relative pronoun, with the prepositional phrase as its complement, and "wadi'ah" as the predicate of "ma." But when he says, "nor anything else," the negation becomes definite.

Hammad ibn Salamah also said: I heard Iyas ibn Mu'awiyah speak concerning a man who took a pledge (rahn). The pledgee said: "I pledged it for ten," and the pledgor said: "I pledged it for five." He said: "If the pledgor has evidence that he handed the pledge over, then the word is that of the pledgor. If he has no evidence of handing over the pledge, and the pledge is in the pledgee's hand, then the word is that of the pledgee, because if he wished he could have denied the pledge altogether."

I say: This is a third opinion on the matter, and it is one of the finest opinions, for his acknowledgment of the pledge, while it is in his hand and the pledgor has no evidence, is a sign of his truthfulness and that he is in the right; had he been a wrongdoer, he would have denied the pledge outright. Malik and our Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on them both, make the word that of the pledgee so long as the claim does not exceed the value of the pledge; al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah and Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on them all, make the word that of the pledgor absolutely.

Iyas also said: Whoever acknowledges something, and there is no evidence against him, the word is what he says.

This too is among the finest judgments, for his acknowledgment is a sign of his truthfulness. If one claims a thousand from him, and has no evidence, and he says: "He is right, except that I have paid it to him," the word is his, and likewise if he acknowledges that he received a trust from his deceased, and has no evidence, and claims that he returned it to him.

Ibrahim ibn Marzuq al-Basri said: Two men came to Iyas ibn Mu'awiyah disputing over two coverlets, one red and the other green. One of them said: "I entered the pool to wash, and I placed my coverlet down. Then this man came and placed his coverlet beneath mine. Then he entered and washed, and he came out before me, took my coverlet and went off with it. Then I came out and followed him, and he claimed that it was his coverlet." He said: "Do you have evidence?" He said: "No." He said: "Bring me a comb." A comb was brought, and he combed the head of this man and the head of that man. Red wool came out from the head of one of them, and green wool from the head of the other. He ruled the red one to the one from whose head the red wool came out, and the green one to the one from whose head the green wool came out.

Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman said, from Zayd Abu 'Ala': I witnessed Iyas ibn Mu'awiyah when two men disputed before him. One said: "He sold me a foolish slave-girl." Iyas said: "And what might this foolishness be?" He said: "Something like madness." Iyas said: "O slave-girl, do you remember when you were born?" She said: "Yes." He said: "Which of your legs is longer?" She said: "This one." Iyas said: "Return her, for she is mad."

Abu al-Hasan al-Mada'ini said, from 'Abd Allah ibn Mus'ab: Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah bore witness before his son Iyas ibn Mu'awiyah, together with men whom he had vouched for, against a man for four thousand dirhams. The one against whom the testimony was given said: "O Abu Wa'ilah, be careful in my matter, for by Allah I only had them witness for two thousand." Iyas asked his father and the witnesses: "Was there any blank space on the document on which they testified?" They said: "Yes; the writing was at the top, the fold was in the middle, and the rest of the document was blank." He said: "Did the one in whose favour the testimony was given meet you at times, and remind you of your testimony of four thousand dirhams?" They said: "Yes, he kept meeting us and saying: 'Remember your testimony against so-and-so for four thousand dirhams.'" He dismissed them and summoned the one in whose favour the testimony was given. He said: "O enemy of Allah, you deceived righteous and heedless people. You had them witness a document, placing the fold in its middle and leaving blank space at its bottom. When they sealed the fold, you cut off the writing in which your right was two thousand dirhams, and you wrote four thousand in the blank space, so the fold came to be at the end of the writing. Then you kept meeting them and prompting them, reminding them that it was four thousand." He acknowledged this and asked him to conceal the matter, and he ruled in his favour for two thousand and concealed the matter.

Nu'aym ibn Hammad said, from Ibrahim ibn Marzuq al-Basri: We were with Iyas ibn Mu'awiyah before he was appointed judge, and we used to write down his insight just as we wrote down hadith from a narrator. A man came and sat on a raised bench at al-Mirbad, and began watching the road. While he was like that, he came down, met a man, looked at his face, then returned to his place. Iyas said: "Say something about this man." They said: "What should we say? A man seeking a need." He said: "He is a teacher of children; a one-eyed slave of his has run away." One of us went to him and asked about his need. He said: "I have a runaway slave." They said: "What is his description?" He said: "Such and such, and one of his eyes is gone." We said: "And what is your occupation?" He said: "I teach children." We said to Iyas: "How did you know that?" He said: "I saw him come and look for a place to sit, and he looked at the highest thing he could reach and sat on it. I considered his standing, and it was not the standing of kings. I considered those who are accustomed to sitting like kings, and I found none but teachers." We said: "How did you know that a slave of his had run away?" He said: "I saw him watching the road, looking into the faces of people." We said: "How did you know that he was one-eyed?" He said: "While he was like that, he came down and met a man who had lost one of his eyes, so I knew that he had mistaken him for his slave."

Al-Harith ibn Murrah said: Iyas ibn Mu'awiyah looked at a man and said: "This man is a stranger, and he is from the people of Wasit. He is a teacher, and he is searching for a runaway slave of his." They found the matter as he had said. They asked him, and he said: "I saw him walking and looking about, so I knew he was a stranger. I saw on his clothing the reddish earth of Wasit, so I knew he was from there. I saw him pass by children and greet them, and not greet men, so I knew he was a teacher. I saw that when he passed by someone of dignified appearance he did not turn to him, and when he passed by someone in rags he studied him, so I knew he was looking for a runaway."

Hilal ibn al-'Ala' al-Raqqi said, from al-Qasim ibn Mansur, from 'Amr ibn Bukayr: Iyas ibn Mu'awiyah passed by and heard a recitation from an upper room, and said: "This is the recitation of a woman pregnant with a boy." He was asked: "How did you know that?" He said: "I heard her voice and her breath mingling, so I knew she was pregnant, and I heard a hoarseness, so I knew that the child was a boy." Then after that he passed by a school in which there were children, looked at one of them, and said: "This is the son of that woman." It was as he said.

A man said to Iyas ibn Mu'awiyah: "Teach me judgment." He said: "Judgment cannot be taught; judgment is understanding. But say: 'Teach me some knowledge,'" and this is the secret of the matter, for Allah, glorified and exalted, says: ﴿And David and Solomon, when they gave judgment concerning the field, when the sheep of the people pastured in it by night, and We were witnesses to their judgment﴾ [al-Anbiya: 78] ﴿So We gave Solomon understanding of it; and to each We gave judgment and knowledge﴾ [al-Anbiya: 79]. Thus He singled out Solomon for the understanding of the case, and generalised knowledge to both of them. Likewise 'Umar wrote to his judge Abu Musa in his well-known letter: "Understanding, understanding in what is presented to you."

What Iyas and Shurayh were distinguished by, together with their sharing of knowledge with the people of their age, is understanding in actual cases, and deriving inference from indications and circumstantial evidence.

This is what escaped many judges, and so they lost many rights.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 21, verse 78–79 (part 1 of 3):

Mention of the two noble Prophets, and praise of them for judgment and knowledge, and the specification of one of them with understanding the case.

(A benefit)

The judge (qadi) and the mufti (jurist who issues legal opinions) share the fact that each of them must make clear the ruling of the Sharia on the matter, but the judge is distinguished by enforcing it and executing it. Accordingly, the conditions for the judge return to the conditions of the witness, the mufti, and the governor: he reports the ruling of the Lawgiver by his knowledge, is accepted by his uprightness, and executes it by his power.

[Chapter: The judgment of the two noble Prophets, Dawud and Sulayman]

Al-harth (الحَرْث) is the orchard. It has been narrated that it was a vineyard, which is called al-karm. Al-nafsh (النَّفْش) is the grazing of sheep at night. Dawud judged by the value of what was destroyed, so he assessed the sheep and found them equal in value to the damage, and he handed them over to the owners of the field, either because they had no dirhams, or because selling them was impossible, and they agreed to take them in place of the value, and those (the owners of the sheep) agreed to hand them over as a substitute for the value.

As for Sulayman, he ruled that the owners of the sheep were liable and must compensate by the equivalent: by restoring the orchard until it returns as it was. He did not deprive them of the produce lost due to the destruction until the time of its return; rather, he gave the owners of the orchard the flock of those people so that they could take from its increase in proportion to the increase of the orchard, thus obtaining from the increase of their sheep the equivalent of what they had lost of the increase of their field. He considered the two increases and found them equal. This is the knowledge which Allah specified for him and praised him for grasping.

The scholars of the Muslims have disputed over such a case in four opinions:

The first: agreement with the Sulaymanic ruling regarding liability for the nafsh and regarding compensation by the equivalent. This is the truth. It is one of the two opinions in the school of Ahmad, and a view of the Shafi'is and Malikis, though the well-known position among them is otherwise.

The second opinion: agreement with him regarding liability for the nafsh, but not regarding compensation by the equivalent. This is the well-known position of the schools of Malik, al-Shafi'i and Ahmad.

The third: agreement with him regarding compensation by the equivalent, but not regarding the nafsh, as when its owner grazed it by his own choice, as opposed to when it strayed and he was unaware of it. This is the opinion of Dawud and those who agree with him.

The fourth opinion: that the nafsh does not create liability in any case, and what is due from the shepherd's liability other than for nafsh is compensated by value, not by equivalent. This is the school of Abu Hanifa.

What the Prophet of Allah Sulayman ruled is the closest to justice and analogy. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ruled that the owners of orchards must guard them by day, and that what livestock destroys at night is a liability on its owners. Thus by his ruling the liability for nafsh is established, and by the previous texts and sound analogy the liability by equivalent is established, and by the text of the Book the praise of Sulayman for understanding this ruling is established. So it is established that it is correct, and success is from Allah.

[Chapter: The level of understanding]

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Dawud and Sulayman, when they judged concerning the field when the sheep of a people grazed in it by night, and We were witnesses to their judgment. And We gave understanding of it to Sulayman, and to each We gave judgment and knowledge.﴾ [al-Anbiya: 78–79]

So He mentioned these two noble Prophets, praised them for knowledge and judgment, and specified Sulayman with understanding in this particular case. Ali ibn Abi Talib, when asked, "Did the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) specify you with anything apart from the people?" said: "No, by Him who split the grain and created the soul, except an understanding which Allah gives a servant in His Book, and what is in this document." And in it was the diya (blood money), the ransom of captives, and that a Muslim is not to be killed for a disbeliever.

In the letter of Umar ibn al-Khattab to Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, may Allah be pleased with both of them: "And understanding, understanding in what is presented to you." Understanding is a blessing from Allah upon His servant, and a light which Allah casts into his heart, by which he recognizes and perceives what others do not perceive or recognize, so he understands from the text what others do not understand, despite both being equal in memorizing it and in understanding its basic meaning.

Thus understanding from Allah and His Messenger is the sign of sincerity (siddiqiyya) and the banner of prophetic guardianship. In it the ranks of scholars vary, to the point that one is counted as a thousand. Consider the understanding of Ibn Abbas, when Umar asked him and those present from the people of Badr and others about the surah ﴿When the help of Allah comes and the victory﴾ [al-Nasr: 1], and what Ibn Abbas was specified with in understanding from it: that it is Allah's notification to His Prophet of his own death and informing him of the approach of his term, and Umar's agreement with him on that, and its being hidden from others of the Companions, though Ibn Abbas was the youngest of them in age at that time. Where would you find in this surah the announcement of his term, were it not for special understanding? This subtlety goes deep, reaching levels which the understanding of most people falls short of, so that with the text they need something else, and the text alone does not suffice for them; but for the one with understanding, he does not need anything beyond the texts.

[Chapter: Examples of judgment by insight and indicators]

Among judgment by insight and indicators is what Muhammad ibn Ubayd Allah ibn Abi Rafi' narrated from his father, who said: A young man from the Ansar brought a case against his mother to Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him. She denied him, so he asked him for evidence, but he had none. The woman brought a group who testified that she had not married and that the young man was lying about her, and that he had slandered her.

Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, ordered him to be flogged. Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, met him and asked about their matter, and he was informed. He summoned them, then sat in the mosque of the Prophet (ﷺ) and questioned the woman, and she denied it. He said to the young man: "Deny her as she denied you." He said: "O cousin of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), she is my mother." He said: "Deny her, and I am your father, and al-Hasan and al-Husayn are your brothers." He said: "I have denied her and rejected her."

Ali said to the guardians of the woman: "Is my decision regarding this woman permissible?" They said: "Yes, and it is also in our hands." Ali said: "I call upon those present to witness that I have married this young man to this woman, who is a stranger to him." "O Qanbar, bring me a pouch containing a dirham." He brought it, and he counted four hundred and eighty dirhams, and gave them to her as her dower.

He said to the young man: "Take the hand of your wife, and do not come to us except with the mark of the wedding upon you." When he turned away, the woman said: "O Abu al-Hasan, by Allah, the Fire! By Allah, he is my son."

He said: "How is that?" She said: "His father was a Zanji (African), and my brothers married me to him, and I conceived this boy. The man went out to fight and was killed, and I sent this boy to the clan of Bani Fulan. He grew up among them, and I was ashamed for him to be my son." Ali said: "I am Abu al-Hasan," and he attached him to her, and his lineage was established.

Among that also: Umar ibn al-Khattab asked a man: "How are you?" He said: "One who loves strife, hates the truth, and testifies to what he has not seen." So Umar ordered him to prison. Ali ordered his release, and said: "He has spoken truly." He said: "How did you judge him truthful?" He said: "He loves wealth and children."

Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿Your wealth and your children are only a trial﴾ [al-Taghabun: 15]. "He hates death, which is the truth. He testifies that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), though he has not seen him." So Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, ordered his release, and said: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am: 124].

Ja'far ibn Muhammad said: Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, was brought a woman who had become attached to a young man of the Ansar, and she loved him. When he did not comply with her, she schemed against him: she took an egg, broke it, discarded the yolk, and poured the white over her garment and between her thighs. Then she came to Umar crying out, saying: "This man overpowered me against my will, and disgraced me before my family, and this is the trace of his deed." Umar asked the women, and they said to him: "Indeed, there is on her body and garment a trace of semen." He resolved to punish the young man, and he began to plead, saying: "O Commander of the Faithful, reflect on my matter, for by Allah I did not commit an immoral act, nor did I intend it. She sought to seduce me, but I refrained." Umar said: "O Abu al-Hasan, what do you see regarding their matter?" Ali looked at what was on the garment. Then he called for water, very hot and boiling, and poured it on the garment, and that white substance congealed. He took it, smelled it and tasted it, and recognized the taste of egg white, and rebuked the woman, and she confessed.

I say: Similar to this is what al-Khiraqi and others narrated from Ahmad: that if a woman claims that her husband is impotent, and he denies it, and she is a non-virgin, then he is left alone with her in a room, and it is said to him: "Release your fluid onto something." If she claims that it is not semen, it is placed over fire; if it melts, it is semen, and her claim is refuted. This is the position of Ata ibn Abi Rabah. This is a judgment by apparent indicators, for semen when placed over fire melts and dissolves, whereas if it is egg white it congeals and dries. If he says, "I am unable to release my fluid," her claim is upheld.

Asbagh ibn Nubata said: A young man complained to Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, about a group of men, saying: "These people went out with my father on a journey. They returned, but my father did not return. I asked them about him, and they said: 'He died.' I asked them about his wealth, and they said: 'He left nothing,' though he had much wealth with him." We brought the matter to Shurayh, who made them swear oaths and released them. Ali then summoned the guards, assigned two men to each man, and instructed them not to allow any of them to approach another, nor to let anyone speak to them. He summoned his scribe, and summoned one of them.

He said: "Tell me about this young man's father: On what day did he go out with you? At what station did you halt? How was your journey? Of what illness did he die? How was his wealth taken? And who washed and buried him? Who led the prayer over him? And where was he buried?" and similar questions, while the scribe wrote. Then Ali said "Allahu akbar," and those present said it too, and the accused, who had no knowledge, assumed that their companion had confessed against them. Then he summoned another after removing the first from the assembly, and asked him as he had asked his companion, then the third likewise, until he knew what all had. He found that each one reported the opposite of what his companion had reported. Then he ordered the first to be brought back, and said: "O enemy of Allah, I have recognized your treachery and lying through what I heard from your companions, and nothing will save you from punishment except truthfulness." Then he ordered him to prison, and said "Allahu akbar," and those present said it with him. When the people saw the situation, they did not doubt that their companion had confessed against them. He summoned another of them and threatened him, and he said: "O Commander of the Faithful, by Allah, I was averse to what they did." Then he summoned all of them, and they confessed to the account. The one in prison was brought out, and it was said to him: "Your companions have confessed, and nothing will save you but truthfulness," so he confessed like the others. So he made them pay the wealth, and carried out retaliation against them for the killing.

A man was brought before one of the judges who had struck another man on the head. The one who was struck claimed that he had destroyed his sight and sense of smell. The judge said: "He is to be tested: he should raise his eyes to the disc of the sun. If he is sound, his eyes do not stay fixed upon it, and tears flow from them. A cloth is burned and brought to his nose. If his sense of smell is sound, the smell reaches his nasal passage and his eyes water."

I saw in "The Judgments of Ali, may Allah be pleased with him" a parallel to this case, in which the one who was struck claimed he was mute. He ordered that his tongue be brought out and pricked with a needle: if the blood that comes out is red, he is sound of tongue; if it comes out black, he is mute.

Asbagh ibn Nubata said: Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, was asked about the ransom of Muslim captives from the hands of the polytheists. He said: "Call out for those whose wounds are in front of them, not those whose wounds are behind them, for that one is a fleer."

Ali also judged in the case of a woman who married; on the night of her wedding she secretly admitted her lover into the bridal chamber. The husband came and entered the chamber, and the lover leapt at him and they fought, and the husband killed the lover. Then the woman stood up against him and killed him. Ali ruled the blood money of the lover against the woman, then he executed her for the husband. He ruled the blood money of the lover against her because she was the one who had exposed him to killing the husband; she was the cause of his death, and she was more deserving of liability than the husband who directly did it, because the one who directly did it killed him in a permitted manner, in defense of his honor. This is among the finest judgments, which many jurists do not arrive at, and it is the correct one.

And he (ʿUmar or the judge, as the text reports) ruled concerning a man who fled from another man who wanted to kill him, and a third man held him in place for him until he caught up and killed him. Nearby was a man who watched them both while he was able to rescue him, but he stood and watched until he was killed. So he ruled that the killer be executed, that the one who held him be imprisoned until he dies, and that the eye of the watcher who stood by and did not object be put out.

Amir al-Mu'minin ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, ruled concerning a man who cut off his wife's genitals: the full diyah (blood money) for the genitals is to be taken from him, and he is to be compelled to keep her until she dies. If he divorces her, he must still maintain her financially.

How excellent this judgment is, and how close it is to the truth! As for the genitals, the full diyah is due for them by consensus (ijma'). As for his maintaining her if he divorces her, that is because he has ruined her for the husbands who would have supported her and provided for her needs, a ruin that never returns. As for compelling him to keep her, it is a punishment for him with the opposite of his intent, for he intended to be rid of her by a forbidden means, while he could have been rid of her by talaq (divorce) or khul' (divorce initiated by the wife through compensation). Instead he turned away from that to this vile mutilation, so his recompense is to be bound to keeping her until death.

He also ruled concerning a newborn who had two heads and two chests on one torso. They asked him: Is he to inherit the inheritance of two people or of one? He said: Leave him until he sleeps, then call out to him. If both wake together, he has the inheritance of one; if one wakes and the other remains asleep, he has the inheritance of two.

Among such cases: ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, was brought a woman who had committed zina (unlawful intercourse). He questioned her and she confessed, so he ordered her stoned. ʿAli said: Perhaps she has an excuse. Then he said to her: What drove you to fornication? She said: I had a partner, and his camels had water and milk, while my camels had no water or milk. I became thirsty and asked him for a drink, but he refused to give me any until I gave him myself. I refused him three times. When I became very thirsty and thought my soul would leave me, I gave him what he wanted, and he gave me to drink. Then ʿAli said: Allahu Akbar! ﴿But whoever is compelled, neither desiring it nor exceeding the limit, there is no sin upon him. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 173].

Also among the judgments of ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him: a man was brought to him who had been found in a ruined house with a knife in his hand stained with blood, and before him was a slain man writhing in his blood. He questioned him, and he said: I killed him. ʿAli said: Take him and kill him. As he was being taken away, a man came running and said: O people, do not hurry! Bring him back to ʿAli. They brought him back, and the man said: O Amir al-Mu'minin, this is not his companion; I killed him. ʿAli said to the first man: What led you to say, "I am his killer," when you did not kill him? He said: O Amir al-Mu'minin, what could I do? The night watch (ʿasas) found the man writhing in his blood, while I was standing with a knife in my hand bearing traces of blood, and I had been seized in a ruined house. I feared that my word would not be accepted, and that this would be a qasamah (the oath procedure in cases of homicide), so I confessed to what I had not done, and I sought my reward with Allah.

ʿAli said: What you did was wretched. So what was your account? He said: I am a butcher. I went out to my shop in the dawn darkness, slaughtered a cow, and skinned it. While I was skinning it with the knife in my hand, I needed to urinate. I came to a ruined house nearby, entered it, relieved myself, and then returned, intending to go to my shop. Suddenly I saw this slain man writhing in his blood, and his condition frightened me. I stood looking at him with the knife in my hand, and I did not realize anything until your companions had stood over me and seized me. The people said: This one killed this one, and there is no killer for him other than him. I became certain that you would not abandon their word for my word, so I confessed to what I had not committed.

ʿAli then said to the second confessor: And what was your story? He said: Iblis (Satan) led me astray. I killed the man out of greed for his wealth. Then I heard the sound of the night watch, so I came out of the ruined house and encountered this butcher in the state he described. I hid from him behind part of the ruin until the night watch came, seized him, and brought him to you. When you ordered his execution, I knew that I would bear his blood as well, so I confessed to the truth.

Then ʿAli said to al-Hasan: What is the ruling concerning him? Al-Hasan said: O Amir al-Mu'minin, if he killed a soul, he has given life to a soul, and Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿And whoever saves one, it is as if he had saved all of mankind﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 32]. So ʿAli released both of them and paid the diyah for the slain man from the public treasury (bayt al-mal).

Four women came before Iyas ibn Muʿawiyah. Iyas said: One of them is pregnant, another is nursing, another is a thayyib (previously married woman), and another is a virgin (bikr). They looked and found the matter just as he had said. They said: How did you know? He said: As for the pregnant one, she was speaking to me while lifting her garment from her belly, so I knew she was pregnant. As for the nursing one, she was striking her breast, so I knew she was nursing. As for the thayyib, she was speaking to me with her eyes meeting mine, so I knew she was a thayyib. As for the virgin, she was speaking to me with her eyes on the ground, so I knew she was a virgin.

Al-Mada'ini related from Rawh: A man from among the trustworthy people deposited money with a man. Later he returned and asked for his deposit, but the man denied it. So he went to Iyas and told him. Iyas said to him: Go away, keep your matter secret, and do not let him know that you came to me. Then return to me after two days. Iyas then summoned the depositary and said: A large amount of money has come, and I want to hand it over to you. Is your house spacious? He said: Yes. He said: Prepare a place for it and porters. The man returned to Iyas, and Iyas said: Go to your companion and ask for the money. If he gives it to you, well and good; if he denies you, say to him: I will inform the judge. So the man went to his companion and said: Give me my money, or I will go to the judge, complain to him, and inform him of my affair. So the man handed over his money. The depositary returned to Iyas and said: He has given me the money. When the trustee came to Iyas for his appointment, Iyas rebuked and scolded him, and said: Do not come near me, you traitor!

Yazid ibn Harun, may Allah have mercy on him, said: A trustworthy man was appointed in Wasit. A man deposited a sealed bag with one of his witnesses and mentioned that it contained a thousand dinars. When the owner's absence was prolonged, the witness opened the bag from its bottom, took the dinars, put dirhams in their place, and resewed it as it had been. Then the owner came, asked for his deposit, and the witness handed him the bag with its seal unchanged. When he opened it and saw the state of affairs, he returned to the witness and said: I deposited dinars with you, and what you gave me is dirhams. The witness said: It is your bag with your seal. So the owner sought the judge's help against him. The judge ordered the depositary to be brought. When they stood before him, the judge said: Since when did he deposit this bag with you? He said: Fifteen years ago. The judge took those dirhams and read their minting, and found that they had been struck two or three years earlier. So he ordered him to hand over the dinars to the owner, dismissed him from his post, and proclaimed his disgrace.

A man deposited money with another man, who denied it. The owner brought the matter to Iyas. Iyas asked him, and he denied it. Iyas said to the claimant: Where did you hand it over to him? He said: In a place in the desert. Iyas said: And what was there? He said: A tree. Iyas said: Go to it, perhaps you buried the money near it and forgot, and you will remember when you see the tree. So he went off. Iyas said to the opponent: Sit until your companion returns. Iyas continued judging, and every so often he looked at him. Then he said to him: Tell me, do you see that your companion has reached the place of the tree? He said: No. Iyas said: O enemy of Allah, you are a traitor! The man said: Forgive me! Iyas said: May Allah not forgive you. He ordered that he be held in custody until the man returned, and Iyas said to him: Go with him and take your right.

A similar case occurred with another judge: a man claimed before him that he had handed a debtor money as a deposit, and the debtor denied it. The judge said to him: Where did you hand it over to him? He said: In a mosque far from the town. The judge said: Go and bring me a copy of the Qur'an from it, so that I may make him swear upon it. The man went off. The judge detained the debtor and then said to him: Do you think he has reached the mosque yet? He said: No. So the judge held him liable for the money.

Judge Abu Hazim had, in such matters, remarkable wonders, and people would object to him, but then the truth would become clear in what he did.

Makram ibn Ahmad said: I was in the assembly of the judge Abu Hazim when an old man came forward with a young boy, and the old man claimed a debt of a thousand dinars against him. He said: What do you say? The boy said: Yes. The judge said to the old man: What do you want? He said: His imprisonment. The judge said: No. The old man said: If the judge sees fit to imprison him, it is more likely to secure my money. Abu Hazim studied them both for a while, then said: Remain bound to one another until I look into your matter at another session. I said to him: Why did you postpone his imprisonment? He said: Woe to you! In most situations I can recognize in the faces of litigants the face of the one who is right from the one who is wrong, and I have acquired a discernment in this that rarely errs. It has occurred to me that this young man's readiness to confess is a sign of his lying, and perhaps the matter will become clear to me so that I may proceed with insight. Do you not see how little these two investigate the denial, how little they dispute, and how calm their temperaments are despite the great amount of money? The habit of youths is not to be excessively scrupulous until someone like this confesses readily and quickly, with a content heart concerning this money. He said: While we were talking like this, the gatekeeper came asking permission to enter for one of the merchants. The judge allowed him. When he entered he said: May Allah set the judge right! I have been afflicted with a young son who squanders every bit of money he gets from me on singing girls with so-and-so. When I prevent him, he devises stratagems that force me to take on his debts. Today the owner of the singing girls has come forward, demanding a thousand dinars immediately, and I have heard that he has approached the judge to have him confess so that he can imprison him. And he is in trouble with his mother, which embitters our life until I settle his debts. When I heard of this, I hurried to the judge to explain his situation. The judge smiled and said to me: How did you see it? I said: This is from Allah's favor upon the judge. He said: Bring me the young man and the old man. Abu Hazim frightened the old man and admonished the young man. They confessed, and the man took his son and left.

Abu al-Sa'ib said: In our town there was a man of concealed condition (mastur al-hal), and the judge wished to accept his testimony. He inquired about him, and he was praised to him both privately and publicly. So the judge summoned him to attend the session to give testimony. The judge sat, and the man attended. When he came to give his testimony, the judge did not accept it. He was asked about the reason, and he said: It became clear to me that he is a hypocrite (murai), so I could not accept his word. He was asked: From where did you know that? He said: He used to come to me every day, and I would count his steps from the point where my eye first fell on him at the door until he reached my seat. When I summoned him today and he came, I counted his steps from that same point, and they had increased by three or about that. So I knew he was affecting something, and I did not accept him.

Ibn Qutaybah said: al-Farazdaq testified before some of the judges, and he said: We have accepted the testimony of Abu Firas and Zaydun. When he left, he was told: By Allah, he did not accept your testimony.

Allah's insight belongs to the one who is the imam of those who discern and the shaykh of those who read signs: ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, whose insight never erred, and who judged among the Ummah by insight supported by revelation.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 21, verse 78–79 (part 3 of 3):

Al-Layth ibn Sa'd said: One day, a beardless youth was brought to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who had been found slain, thrown on the side of the road. 'Umar inquired about his matter and made every effort, but he could not come upon any information about it, and this grieved him. So he said: "O Allah, grant me victory over his killer." Then, when a full year had passed, an infant was found, newly born, thrown at the place where the slain man had been. He was brought to 'Umar, who said: "By Allah's will, I have obtained retribution for the blood of the slain man." He gave the infant to a woman and said to her: "Look after him, take his maintenance from us, and watch who takes him from you. When you find a woman who kisses him and presses him to her breast, inform me of her whereabouts."

When the infant grew up, a slave girl came and said to the woman: "My mistress has sent me to you so that you may send the boy to her, so that she may see him and return him to you." The woman said: "Yes, go with him to her, and I will accompany you." So she went with the boy, the woman accompanying her, until they entered upon her mistress. When she saw him, she took him, kissed him and pressed him to her. Behold, she was the daughter of an old man from the Ansar, one of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The woman went to 'Umar and informed him. He girded on his sword and went to the woman's house. He found her father reclining at the door of his house, and he said to him: "O so-and-so, what has your daughter, so-and-so, done?"

He said: "May Allah reward her with good, O Commander of the Faithful. She is among the people most knowing of the right of Allah and the right of her father, along with her good prayer, her fasting, and her upholding of her religion." 'Umar said: "I wish to enter upon her, so that I may increase her desire for good and urge her toward it." So her father entered, and 'Umar entered with him. 'Umar ordered those with her to leave, and they departed, and he and the woman remained in the house. 'Umar uncovered the sword and said: "Be truthful with me, or I will strike off your neck," and he never lied. She said: "Be patient. By Allah, I will speak the truth: an old woman used to visit me, and I took her as a mother, and she would attend to my affairs as a mother does. I was to her like a daughter, until a period passed. Then she said: 'O my daughter, a journey has come up for me, and I have a daughter in a place where I fear she may be lost. I wish to entrust her to you until I return from my journey.' Then she took a son of hers, a young beardless youth, dressed him in the likeness of a girl, and brought him to me, and I had no doubt that he was a girl. So he would see from me what a girl sees from a girl, until one day he caught me unawares while I was asleep. I did not perceive until he had mounted me and penetrated me. I stretched my hand to a knife that was at my side, and I killed him."

Then I ordered that he be cast away wherever I saw fit, and I conceived this infant from him. When I gave birth, I cast him at the place of his father. This, by Allah, is their story as I have informed you." He said: "You have spoken the truth." Then he counselled her, prayed for her, and departed. He said to her father: "What an excellent daughter you have!" Then he left.

Among such instances is the insight (firasah) of Ibn 'Umar concerning al-Husayn when he bade him farewell and said: "I entrust you to Allah from being slain," while he had with him the letters of the people of Iraq. Ibn 'Umar's insight was more truthful than their letters.

Among such instances: two men from Quraysh deposited with a woman one hundred dinars as a trust, and said: "Do not hand it over to either of us without the other." They remained for a year, then one of them came and said: "My companion has died, so hand the dinars over to me." She refused and said: "You both told me, 'Do not hand it over to either of us without the other,' so I will not hand it over to you." She was pressed by her family and neighbours until she handed it over to him. Then she remained another year, and the other came and said: "Hand over the dinars to me." She said: "Your companion came to me and claimed that you had died, so I handed it over to him." They disputed before 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and he intended to rule against her. She said: "Refer us to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib." 'Ali realised that the two had deceived her, and said: "Did you not both say, 'Do not hand it over to either of us without the other'?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Then your property is with her. Go and bring your companion, so that she may hand it over to you both."

[Chapter: On the insight of the judge]

Among the insight of the judge is what Hammad ibn Salamah related from Humayd al-Tawil: that two men disputed before Iyas ibn Mu'awiyah, one of whom had deposited a trust with his companion. The owner of the trust said: "Make him swear by Allah that I have no trust with him." Iyas said: "Rather, I will make him swear by Allah that you have no trust with him, nor anything else."

This is among the finest insight, for if he says, "I have no trust with him," it admits of negation, and also of affirmation, since one may read "mala" as governed by a verb understood, meaning: he delivered his property to me, or gave me his property; or one may take "ma" as a relative pronoun, with the prepositional phrase as its complement, and "wadi'ah" as the predicate of "ma." But when he says, "nor anything else," the negation becomes definite.

Hammad ibn Salamah also said: I heard Iyas ibn Mu'awiyah speak concerning a man who took a pledge (rahn). The pledgee said: "I pledged it for ten," and the pledgor said: "I pledged it for five." He said: "If the pledgor has evidence that he handed the pledge over, then the word is that of the pledgor. If he has no evidence of handing over the pledge, and the pledge is in the pledgee's hand, then the word is that of the pledgee, because if he wished he could have denied the pledge altogether."

I say: This is a third opinion on the matter, and it is one of the finest opinions, for his acknowledgment of the pledge, while it is in his hand and the pledgor has no evidence, is a sign of his truthfulness and that he is in the right; had he been a wrongdoer, he would have denied the pledge outright. Malik and our Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on them both, make the word that of the pledgee so long as the claim does not exceed the value of the pledge; al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah and Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on them all, make the word that of the pledgor absolutely.

Iyas also said: Whoever acknowledges something, and there is no evidence against him, the word is what he says.

This too is among the finest judgments, for his acknowledgment is a sign of his truthfulness. If one claims a thousand from him, and has no evidence, and he says: "He is right, except that I have paid it to him," the word is his, and likewise if he acknowledges that he received a trust from his deceased, and has no evidence, and claims that he returned it to him.

Ibrahim ibn Marzuq al-Basri said: Two men came to Iyas ibn Mu'awiyah disputing over two coverlets, one red and the other green. One of them said: "I entered the pool to wash, and I placed my coverlet down. Then this man came and placed his coverlet beneath mine. Then he entered and washed, and he came out before me, took my coverlet and went off with it. Then I came out and followed him, and he claimed that it was his coverlet." He said: "Do you have evidence?" He said: "No." He said: "Bring me a comb." A comb was brought, and he combed the head of this man and the head of that man. Red wool came out from the head of one of them, and green wool from the head of the other. He ruled the red one to the one from whose head the red wool came out, and the green one to the one from whose head the green wool came out.

Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman said, from Zayd Abu 'Ala': I witnessed Iyas ibn Mu'awiyah when two men disputed before him. One said: "He sold me a foolish slave-girl." Iyas said: "And what might this foolishness be?" He said: "Something like madness." Iyas said: "O slave-girl, do you remember when you were born?" She said: "Yes." He said: "Which of your legs is longer?" She said: "This one." Iyas said: "Return her, for she is mad."

Abu al-Hasan al-Mada'ini said, from 'Abd Allah ibn Mus'ab: Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah bore witness before his son Iyas ibn Mu'awiyah, together with men whom he had vouched for, against a man for four thousand dirhams. The one against whom the testimony was given said: "O Abu Wa'ilah, be careful in my matter, for by Allah I only had them witness for two thousand." Iyas asked his father and the witnesses: "Was there any blank space on the document on which they testified?" They said: "Yes; the writing was at the top, the fold was in the middle, and the rest of the document was blank." He said: "Did the one in whose favour the testimony was given meet you at times, and remind you of your testimony of four thousand dirhams?" They said: "Yes, he kept meeting us and saying: 'Remember your testimony against so-and-so for four thousand dirhams.'" He dismissed them and summoned the one in whose favour the testimony was given. He said: "O enemy of Allah, you deceived righteous and heedless people. You had them witness a document, placing the fold in its middle and leaving blank space at its bottom. When they sealed the fold, you cut off the writing in which your right was two thousand dirhams, and you wrote four thousand in the blank space, so the fold came to be at the end of the writing. Then you kept meeting them and prompting them, reminding them that it was four thousand." He acknowledged this and asked him to conceal the matter, and he ruled in his favour for two thousand and concealed the matter.

Nu'aym ibn Hammad said, from Ibrahim ibn Marzuq al-Basri: We were with Iyas ibn Mu'awiyah before he was appointed judge, and we used to write down his insight just as we wrote down hadith from a narrator. A man came and sat on a raised bench at al-Mirbad, and began watching the road. While he was like that, he came down, met a man, looked at his face, then returned to his place. Iyas said: "Say something about this man." They said: "What should we say? A man seeking a need." He said: "He is a teacher of children; a one-eyed slave of his has run away." One of us went to him and asked about his need. He said: "I have a runaway slave." They said: "What is his description?" He said: "Such and such, and one of his eyes is gone." We said: "And what is your occupation?" He said: "I teach children." We said to Iyas: "How did you know that?" He said: "I saw him come and look for a place to sit, and he looked at the highest thing he could reach and sat on it. I considered his standing, and it was not the standing of kings. I considered those who are accustomed to sitting like kings, and I found none but teachers." We said: "How did you know that a slave of his had run away?" He said: "I saw him watching the road, looking into the faces of people." We said: "How did you know that he was one-eyed?" He said: "While he was like that, he came down and met a man who had lost one of his eyes, so I knew that he had mistaken him for his slave."

Al-Harith ibn Murrah said: Iyas ibn Mu'awiyah looked at a man and said: "This man is a stranger, and he is from the people of Wasit. He is a teacher, and he is searching for a runaway slave of his." They found the matter as he had said. They asked him, and he said: "I saw him walking and looking about, so I knew he was a stranger. I saw on his clothing the reddish earth of Wasit, so I knew he was from there. I saw him pass by children and greet them, and not greet men, so I knew he was a teacher. I saw that when he passed by someone of dignified appearance he did not turn to him, and when he passed by someone in rags he studied him, so I knew he was looking for a runaway."

Hilal ibn al-'Ala' al-Raqqi said, from al-Qasim ibn Mansur, from 'Amr ibn Bukayr: Iyas ibn Mu'awiyah passed by and heard a recitation from an upper room, and said: "This is the recitation of a woman pregnant with a boy." He was asked: "How did you know that?" He said: "I heard her voice and her breath mingling, so I knew she was pregnant, and I heard a hoarseness, so I knew that the child was a boy." Then after that he passed by a school in which there were children, looked at one of them, and said: "This is the son of that woman." It was as he said.

A man said to Iyas ibn Mu'awiyah: "Teach me judgment." He said: "Judgment cannot be taught; judgment is understanding. But say: 'Teach me some knowledge,'" and this is the secret of the matter, for Allah, glorified and exalted, says: ﴿And David and Solomon, when they gave judgment concerning the field, when the sheep of the people pastured in it by night, and We were witnesses to their judgment﴾ [al-Anbiya: 78] ﴿So We gave Solomon understanding of it; and to each We gave judgment and knowledge﴾ [al-Anbiya: 79]. Thus He singled out Solomon for the understanding of the case, and generalised knowledge to both of them. Likewise 'Umar wrote to his judge Abu Musa in his well-known letter: "Understanding, understanding in what is presented to you."

What Iyas and Shurayh were distinguished by, together with their sharing of knowledge with the people of their age, is understanding in actual cases, and deriving inference from indications and circumstantial evidence.

This is what escaped many judges, and so they lost many rights.

(Benefit)

In this supplication he combined the reality of tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness), the display of need and poverty before one's Lord, the taste of love in humbly appealing to Him, the acknowledgment of His attribute of mercy and that He is the Most Merciful of the merciful, seeking nearness to Him through His attributes (ﷻ), and the intensity of one's need, which is one's poverty. Whenever the afflicted person attains this, his affliction is lifted from him.

It has been tested that whoever says it seven times, especially with this knowledge, God removes his harm.

[Section: The difference between reporting one's condition and complaining]

The difference between reporting one's condition and complaining, although their outward forms may resemble each other, is this: reporting one's condition is done with a sound intention, such as informing someone of the cause of his indebtedness, or excusing oneself to one's brother for a request he has made, or warning him against falling into what one has fallen into, so that the one who reports is advising him by his report, or encouraging him to patience through example. It is related about al-Ahnaf that a man complained to him, and he said: "O nephew, the light of my eye went out so-and-so many years ago, and I have not informed anyone of it."

Within this report there is encouragement of the complainer to patience and endurance, for which the one who reports is rewarded. Its form resembles a complaint, but the intention distinguishes between them. Perhaps this is the meaning of the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) when 'A'isha said, "Oh, my head!" and he said, "Rather, I am the one who has the headache!"

That is, the severe pain is in me, not you, so take me as an example and do not complain. There appears to me another meaning in it: she was the beloved of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), indeed she was the most beloved of women to him without qualification.

So when she complained to him of her head, he informed her that the lover feels pain like that which she feels. This is the utmost in agreement between a lover and his beloved: he suffers when she suffers and rejoices when she rejoices, so that if a limb of hers pains him, the lover feels pain in that very same limb. This comes from the sincerity of love and the purity of affection. Thus the first meaning is understood as: "Do not complain; be patient, for I am suffering the same pain you suffer, so follow my example in patience and not complaining." The second meaning conveys to her the sincerity of his love, that is: "See the strength of my love for you, how I consoled you in your pain and your headache, so that you were in pain while I was free of pain; rather, what pains you pains me, just as what gladdens you gladdens me," as one has said:

"And the most deserving of creatures to console is the one who consoled you in sorrow."

As for complaint, it is the report that is stripped of a sound intention, rather its source is discontent and the afflicted person's grievance to others. But if he complains to God, glorified and exalted is He, this is not a complaint but an appeal for compassion, supplication and entreaty to Him, like the words of Job to his Lord: ﴿Indeed, harm has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful.﴾

And the words of Jacob: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and my grief to God.﴾

And the words of Moses:

"O God, to You be praise, to You is the complaint, You are the one sought for help, to You is the appeal for aid, upon You is reliance, and there is no power or might except through You."

And the words of the master of the children of Adam (ﷺ):

"O God, to You I complain of the weakness of my strength, the scarcity of my resources, and my humiliation before people. You are Lord of the weak, and You are my Lord. To whom will You entrust me? To a distant one who frowns at me, or to an enemy You have given authority over my affair? If there is no anger from You upon me, I do not mind, but Your well-being is more expansive for me. I seek refuge in the light of Your Face, by which the darkness is illuminated and the affairs of this world and the Hereafter are set right, that Your wrath should descend upon me or Your displeasure should come down upon me. To You is the blame until You are pleased, and there is no power or might except through You."

So complaint to God, glorified be He, does not contradict patience in any way. God, the Exalted, said of Job: ﴿Indeed, We found him patient; an excellent servant, indeed he was ever turning back (to God).﴾ Along with this, He reported of him that he complained to Him, in His words: ﴿Harm has touched me.﴾ And He reported of His prophet Jacob that he promised himself beautiful patience, and a prophet, when he speaks, fulfills his word, along with His words: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and my grief to God﴾, and He did not consider that a deficiency in his patience.

Nor should one pay attention to what is other than this from the nonsense of some people. Some of them said, regarding his words ﴿harm has touched me﴾: God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, We found him patient﴾ and did not say "patient and enduring" in the case where he said ﴿harm has touched me﴾.

Some of them said: He did not say "have mercy on me," but rather said ﴿You are the Most Merciful of the merciful﴾, so he added nothing beyond reporting his own condition and describing his Lord.

Some of them said: He only complained of the touch of harm when his tongue became too weak to remember God, so he complained of the harm of weakness in remembrance, not the harm of illness and pain.

Some of them said: He was prompted to this statement so that he would be an example for the weak of this community.

It seems that this speaker thought that complaint to God contradicts patience, and he erred in the most hideous way. What contradicts patience is his complaint to people, not complaint to Him. God tests His servant in order to hear his humble supplication and his prayer, and complaint to Him is not contrary to this; He does not love that one should show self-restraint before Him. The thing most beloved to Him is the breaking of the heart of His servant before Him, his humbling himself to Him, and his display of weakness, need, helplessness and scarcity of patience. So beware, with the utmost caution, of displaying self-control before Him. Rather, hold fast to humility, submissiveness, showing one's helplessness, need, abasement and weakness, for His mercy is closer to this heart than the hand is to the mouth.

Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary on Surah 21, verses 87–88:

As for the supplication of Dhu'n-Nun (Dhul-Nun, the Man of the Fish, i.e. Prophet Yunus): it contains the perfection of tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness) and tanzih (declaring God far above any imperfection) of the Lord, may He be exalted, and the servant's acknowledgment of his own wrongdoing and sin. It is among the most effective remedies for distress, anxiety and grief, and among the most powerful means to God, glorified is He, for the fulfilment of needs. For tawhid and tanzih comprise the affirmation of every perfection of God and the negation of every deficiency, defect, and likeness to Him.

Acknowledging wrongdoing comprises the servant's faith in the Law (shar'), in reward and in punishment, and it necessitates his humbling himself, his returning to God, his seeking forgiveness for his slip, his acknowledging his servanthood, and his neediness towards his Lord. Thus there are here four matters through which supplication by means (tawassul) has been made: tawhid, tanzih, servanthood ('ubudiyyah), and acknowledgment (i'tiraf).

He said in Ijtima' al-Juyush al-Islamiyyah (The Gathering of the Islamic Armies):

Shaykh Muwaffaq al-Din Ibn Qudamah al-Maqdisi mentioned in his book "Ithbat Sifat al-'Uluw" (Affirmation of the Attribute of Highness), from al-Hasan al-Basri, with a sound chain of narration, that he said: Yunus, peace be upon him, heard the glorification of the pebbles and the fish, so he began to glorify God, and he used to say in his supplication:

"O my Master, in the heaven is Your dwelling, and on the earth is Your power and Your wonders. My God, in the three darknesses You have imprisoned me..." When the forty days were complete and grief afflicted him, ﴿He called out in the darknesses: "There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been of the wrongdoers."﴾

He said in Tariq al-Hijratayn (The Path of the Two Migrations):

This is the station of Dhu'n-Nun when he says: ﴿There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been of the wrongdoers.﴾

So he affirmed the oneness of his Lord, declared Him far above every defect, and attributed the wrong to himself. This is also the station of the master of the "Sayyid al-Istighfar" (the Master of Seeking Forgiveness), when he says in his supplication:

"O God, You are my Lord, there is no god but You. You created me and I am Your servant, and I abide by Your covenant and Your promise as far as I am able. I seek refuge in You from the evil of what I have done. I acknowledge before You Your blessing upon me, and I acknowledge my sin, so forgive me, for none forgives sins but You."

Thus he affirmed Tawhid al-Rububiyyah (oneness of Lordship), which includes His sole creation and the universality and effectiveness of His will, and Tawhid al-Uluhiyyah (oneness of worship), which includes loving Him and worshipping Him alone without partner, and the acknowledgment of servanthood, which includes neediness towards Him in every respect.

(Section)

In the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi and the Sahih of al-Hakim, from the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The supplication of Dhu'n-Nun, when he called while in the belly of the fish: ﴿There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been of the wrongdoers.﴾

No Muslim has ever supplicated with it for anything except that Allah responded to him." Al-Tirmidhi said: This is a sahih hadith.

Also in the Mustadrak of al-Hakim, from the hadith of Sa'd, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Shall I not inform you of something which, when a matter of great importance befalls a man among you and he supplicates with it, Allah relieves him of it? The supplication of Dhu'n-Nun."

Also in his Sahih, from him, that he heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "Shall I guide you to the Greatest Name of Allah? The supplication of Yunus." A man said: "O Messenger of Allah, was it for Yunus alone?" He said: "Do you not hear His saying: ﴿So We answered him and delivered him from distress, and thus do We deliver the believers﴾ [al-Anbiya: 88]? Any Muslim who supplicates with it during his illness forty times, and then dies in that illness, will be given the reward of a martyr, and if he recovers, he will recover forgiven."

Ibn Mas'ud said: No prophet among the prophets was ever afflicted with distress except that he sought relief through glorification (tasbih).
